Gradient flow and entropy inequalities for quantum Markov semigroups with detailed balance
Eric A. Carlen
Address: Department of Mathematics

Abstract.
We study a class of ergodic quantum Markov semigroups on finite-dimensional unital  $C^{*}$ -algebras. These semigroups have a unique stationary state  $\sigma$ , and we are concerned with those that satisfy a quantum detailed balance condition with respect to  $\sigma$ .
We show that the evolution on the set of states that is given by such a quantum Markov semigroup is gradient flow for the relative entropy with respect to  $\sigma$  in a particular Riemannian metric on the set of states.
This metric is a non-commutative analog of the  $2$ -Wasserstein metric, and in several interesting cases we are able to show, in analogy with work of Otto on gradient flows with respect to the classical  $2$ -Wasserstein metric, that the relative entropy is strictly and uniformly convex with respect to the Riemannian metric introduced here.
As a consequence, we obtain a number of new inequalities for the decay of relative entropy for ergodic quantum Markov semigroups with detailed balance.
Keywords: quantum Markov semigroup, entropy, detailed balance, gradient flow.
Subject Classification Numbers: 46L57, 81S22, 34D05, 47C90
1. introduction
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be a finite-dimensional  $C^{*}$ -algebra with unit  ${{\bf 1}}$ .
We may identify  $\mathcal{A}$  with a  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , the  $C^{*}$ -algebra of
$n\times n$  matrices, for some  $n$ .
In finite dimension, there is no difference between weak and norm closure, and so
$\mathcal{A}$  is also a von Neumann algebra.
A Quantum Markov Semigroup (QMS) is a continuous one-parameter semigroup of
linear transformations  $({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  such that for each  $t\geq 0$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is completely positive and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}$ .
Associated to any QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ , is the dual semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}^{\dagger}_{t}$
acting on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ , the set of faithful states of  $\mathcal{A}$ .
(When there is no ambiguity, we simply write  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ .)
The QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is ergodic in case  ${{\bf 1}}$  spans the eigenspace of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  for the eigenvalue  $1$ .
In that case, there is a unique invariant state  $\sigma$ .
While  $\sigma$  need not be faithful, a natural projection operation allows us to assume,
effectively without loss of generality, that  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ . Characterizations of the
generators of quantum Markov semigroups on the  $C^{*}$ -algebra  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$
of all  $n\times n$  matrices were given at the same time by Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudershan
[31], and by Lindblad [46] in a more general setting (but still assuming
norm continuity of the semigroup). Such semigroups are often called Lindblad semigroups.
The notion of detailed balance in the theory of classical Markov processes has
several different quantum counterparts, as discussed below.
One of these is singled out here, with a full discussion of how it relates to other
variants and why it is physically natural.
Suffice it to say here that, as we shall see, the class of ergodic QMS that satisfy the
detailed balance condition includes a wide variety of examples arising in physics.
The set of faithful states  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$  may be identified with the set of invertible density matrices
$\sigma$  on  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$  that belong to  $\mathcal{A}$ , as is recalled below.
For  $\rho,\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ , the relative entropy of  $\rho$  with respect to  $\sigma$  is the functional
(1.1)
$D(\rho\|\sigma)={\rm Tr}[\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)]\ .$
We show in Theorem 7.6 that associated to any QMS
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  satisfying detailed balance, there is a Riemannian metric  $g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  on
${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  such that the flow on
${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  induced by the dual semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$  is
gradient flow for the metric  $g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  of the relative entropy
$D(\cdot\|\sigma)$  with respect to the invariant state  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ .
In several cases, we shall show that the relative entropy functional is geodesically convex for
$g_{\mathcal{L}}$ , and as a consequence, we shall deduce a number of functional
inequalities that are useful for studying the evolution governed by  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ .
In particular, we shall deduce several sharp relative entropy dissipation inequalities.
Some of these are new; see e.g. Theorem 8.5 and Theorem 8.6.
The Riemannian distance corresponding to  $g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  will be seen to be a very natural analog of the
$2$ -Wasserstein distance on the space of probability densities on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$  [73, Chapter 6].
Otto showed [55] that a large number of classical evolution equations could be viewed as gradient flow
in the  $2$ -Wasserstein metric for certain functionals, and that when the functionals were geodesically uniformly convex for this geometry, a host of useful functional inequalities were consequently valid.
This is for instance the case when the functional driving the flow is classical relative entropy with respect to a Gaussian reference measure.
In this case, the flow is given by the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, described by the Fokker-Planck equation with linear drift.
One of the inequalities that is a consequence of the uniform geodesic convexity of the relative entropy is the sharp bound on entropy dissipation for solutions of the Fokker-Planck equation.
The present paper also greatly extends our previous paper [12] in which we obtained a gradient flow structure for the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.
In particular, we prove a sharp geodesic convexity result for the von Neumann entropy in this setting, thereby solving a problem that was left open in [12]. Thus, our results can be viewed as a non-commutative extension of Otto’s investigation of classical gradient flows.
Mielke [50, 51] investigated related variational formulations for dissipative quantum systems based on Öttinger’s so-called GENERIC framework [53, 54].
However, the gradient flow structure considered in Mielke’s papers is in general different from the one introduced in the present paper, as the approach in [50, 51] gives rise to nonlinear evolution equations that are different from the linear Lindblad equations that we obtain here. Also, Junge and Zeng [39] have recently developed an approach to some non-commutative functional inequalities involving a non-commutative analog of the  $1$ -Wasserstein metric.
We restrict our attention to the case that  $\mathcal{A}$  is a finite-dimensional  $C^{*}$ -algebra because this setting already includes many examples of physical interest, and we wish to explain our methods in a way that does not encumber them with the host of technical and topological difficulties that would follow in an infinite-dimensional setting.
For example, in an infinite-dimensional setting, it would matter that  $\mathcal{A}$  is a von Neumann algebra and not only a  $C^{*}$ -algebra with a unit, so that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}$  would have a pre-dual, and then what we call  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$  here would be the set of normal states;
i.e., states that are continuous with respect to the weak- $*$  topology on  $\mathcal{A}$ , and we would require that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  be normal for each  $t$ ;
i.e., continuous with respect to the weak- $*$  topology on  $\mathcal{A}$ .
The innocent formula  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  would require closer scrutiny, and so forth.
Many of the issues involved in extending our results to a more general infinite-dimensional setting are standard but not all of them.
This will be done elsewhere.
We also refer to a forthcoming paper for a treatment of more general transport metrics, general entropy functionals, and their geodesic convexity properties [13].
Here instead, we present a development of our methods that
will be readily understood by people who are interested in the many physically interesting finite-dimensional examples.
We shall also show that our methods may be applied in the infinite-dimensional setting to particular examples without first generalizing the whole theory.
We illustrate this with the family of Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups, which are always infinite-dimensional since all non-trivial representations of the Canonical Commutation Relations are infinite-dimensional.
We use our methods to prove a new sharp relative entropy dissipation inequality for this family that had recently been conjectured in [38]; see Theorem 8.5. We also prove some other sharp inequalities of this type; e.g., Theorem 8.6.
While this introduction has, in the interest of brevity, used a considerable amount of terminology without explanation, the rest of the paper is elementary and quite self-contained.
We do assume a basic familiarity with  $C^{*}$ -algebras, von Neumann algebras and completely positive maps.
Many readers will have this familiarity, but for background on  $C^{*}$  and von Neumann algebras, we refer to Sakai [64], and for completely positive maps to Paulsen [59].
Terminology and facts that are used here without explanation can be found in these references.
We close the introduction with some preliminary definitions and by establishing some notation that will be in use throughout the paper.
1.1. Preliminary definitions and notation
$\mathcal{A}$  will always denote a finite-dimensional  $C^{*}$ -algebra with unit  ${{\bf 1}}$ , regarded as subalgebra of some matrix algebra  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
The center of  $\mathcal{A}$  is generated by a single self-adjoint element  $Z\in\mathcal{A}$ , and its spectral projections yield
a decomposition of  $\mathcal{A}$  into a finite direct sum of factors:
Let  $\{\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{p}\}$  for some  $1\leq p\leq n$  be the distinct eigenvalues of  $Z$ , and let  $\mathcal{H}_{j}$  be the eigenspace with eigenvalue  $\lambda_{j}$ .
Then each  $\mathcal{H}_{j}$  is invariant under  $\mathcal{A}$ , and letting  $\mathcal{A}_{j}$  denote the restriction of  $\mathcal{A}$  to  $\mathcal{H}_{j}$ ,  $\mathcal{A}_{j}$  has a trivial center; that is,  $\mathcal{A}_{j}$  is a factor.
The structure of finite-dimensional factors is well-known:  $\mathcal{H}_{j}$  is unitarily equivalent to  ${\mathbb{C}}^{\ell_{j}}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{r_{j}}$ , and there is a unitary equivalence in which each  $A\in\mathcal{A}_{j}$  takes the form  $I_{\ell_{j}}\otimes\widehat{A}$  where  $\widehat{A}\in\mathcal{M}_{r_{j}}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
That is, each factor may be identified in a natural way with a full matrix algebra.
However, not all finite-dimensional  $C^{*}$ -algebras arising in mathematical physics are factors.
For example, a Clifford algebra with an odd number  $k$  of generators, arising in the description of a system of  $k$  Fermi degrees of freedom, is not a factor.
This example will be discussed in detail later on.
Let  $\tau$  denote the normalized trace on  $A$  given by  $\tau(A)={\rm Tr}[A]/{\rm Tr}[{{\bf 1}}]$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .
Then  $\tau$  is a faithful state on  $\mathcal{A}$ .
Let  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  denote the Hilbert space formed by equipping  $\mathcal{A}$  with the GNS inner product determined by  $\tau$ .
That is, for all  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
$\langle A,B\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=\tau[A^{*}B]\ .$
We could use this inner product to identify  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  with the space of linear functionals on  $\mathcal{A}$ , but to keep contact with the physics literature, we do something slightly different:
We use the un-normalized trace to write the general linear functional  $\varphi$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  in the form
$\varphi(B)={\rm Tr}[AB]$
for some  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .
It is easy to see that  $\varphi$  is a positive linear functional (in the sense that  $\varphi(B)\geq 0$  whenever  $B\geq 0$ ) if and only if  $A\geq 0$  in  $\mathcal{A}$ .
It follows that the set of faithful states on  $\mathcal{A}$  may be identified with the set of
strictly positive elements  $A$  of  $\mathcal{A}$  such that  ${\rm Tr}[A]=1$ .
Since  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  is strictly positive in  $\mathcal{A}$  if and only if it is strictly positive in  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , we may identify the set of faithful states on  $\mathcal{A}$  with the set of invertible density matrices  $\rho$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that belong to the subalgebra  $\mathcal{A}$ .
In the following, we always write  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  to denote this set, whether we think of it as a set of faithful states or as a set of density matrices.
1.1 DEFINITION (Modular operator and modular group).
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ .
Define a linear operator  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ , or, what is the same thing, on  $\mathcal{A}$ , by
$\Delta_{\sigma}(A)=\sigma A\sigma^{-1}$
for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  is called the modular operator. The modular generator is the self-adjoint element  $h\in\mathcal{A}$  given by
$h=-\log\sigma\ .$
The modular automorphism group  $\alpha_{t}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  is the group defined by
(1.2)
$\alpha_{t}(A)=e^{ith}Ae^{-ith}$
for  $t\in{\mathbb{C}}$ . Note that  $\Delta_{\sigma}=\alpha_{i}$ .
The modular operator and the modular automorphism group are central to the characterization of an important class of quantum Markov semigroups.
First, Davies [21] identified a class of quantum Markov semigroups that he rigorously showed to arise from coupling a finite quantum system with internal Hamiltonian  $h$  to an infinite fermion heat bath and then taking a weak coupling limit.
The whole class of quantum Markov semigroups he found has the property that the semigroup commutes with the modular automorphism group  $\alpha_{t}$  given by (1.2) where  $h$  is the internal Hamiltonian, and then  $\sigma=e^{-h}/{\rm Tr}[e^{-h}]$ .
(Note that adding a scalar constant to  $h$  has no effect on (1.2).)
Of course an operator on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  commutes with the modular group if and only if it commutes with the modular operator.
Second, Alicki [5] showed that commutativity with respect to the modular operator is central to one natural extension of the notion of detailed balance from classical Markov chains to the quantum setting.
Before explaining this fact, which is important for our work here, we first introduce some more terminology and notation.
A linear operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  is positivity preserving in case  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A\geq 0$  whenever  $A\geq 0$ .
A linear operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  is self-adjointness preserving in case  $({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*}$ , or, equivalently,
in case  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A$  is self-adjoint whenever  $A$  is self-adjoint.
Evidently, any positivity preserving operator is self-adjointness preserving.
When  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  is a self-adjointness preserving semigroup, then its generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}=\lim_{t\to 0}t^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-I)$  is self-adjointness preserving as well.
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  and note that  $(\Delta_{\sigma}A)^{*}=\Delta_{\sigma}^{-1}(A^{*})$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ . Moreover, for all  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
${\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}B]={\rm Tr}[(\Delta_{\sigma}A)^{*}B]\quad{\rm and}\quad{\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}A]={\rm Tr}[|\sigma^{1/2}A\sigma^{-1/2}|^{2}]\ ,$
so that  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  is a positive operator on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ .
A dagger  $\dagger$  will be used to denote the adjoint with respect to the inner product in  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ , or,
what is the same, with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product.
We will encounter many other inner products on  $\mathcal{A}$ , but the GNS inner product associated to  $\tau$  has a special role.
We may then rewrite one of the conclusions from just above as  $\Delta_{\sigma}^{\dagger}=\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
Because of the self-adjointness of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$
there is an orthonormal basis  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}$  of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  consisting of eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
Since  $\Delta_{\sigma}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}$ , we may always assume that  $E_{1}={{\bf 1}}$ .
In this case,  ${\rm Tr}[E_{\gamma}]=\tau(E_{\gamma})=0$  for all  $\gamma>1$ .
Furthermore, since  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  is strictly positive, all eigenvalues of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  are strictly positive, hence we may write them in the form  $e^{-\omega_{\gamma}}$ .
Since  $(\Delta_{\sigma}A)^{*}=\Delta_{\sigma}^{-1}A^{*}$ , it follows that for all  $E\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ ,
(1.3)
$\Delta_{\sigma}E=e^{-\omega}E\quad\iff\quad\Delta_{\sigma}E^{*}=e^{\omega}E^{*}\ .$
In particular, if for  $\omega\neq 0$ ,  $e^{-\omega}$  is an eigenvalue of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ , then so is  $e^{\omega}$ , and the two eigenspaces are orthogonal and have the same dimension.
It follows that there exists an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  with the properties listed in the next definition:
1.2 DEFINITION (Modular basis).
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be a finite-dimensional  $C^{*}$ -algebra and let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ .
Then there exists an orthonormal basis  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}$  of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  with the following properties:
(i)  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}$  consists of eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
(ii)  $E_{1}={{\bf 1}}$ .
(iiI)  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}=\{E_{1}^{*},\dots,E_{m}^{*}\}$
2. Detailed balance
There is a large literature on the detailed balance condition in a quantum setting, starting with the work of Agarwal [3], which initiated a number of investigations in the 1970’s including
[5, 14, 42, 68]. Already in these papers, one finds several different, and non-equivalent, definitions. A number of more recent investigations [2, 25, 27, 48, 70] have added to the variety
of meanings attached to this term. We therefore carefully explain the context of the definition that we use here, and why it is the most natural for our purposes.
Let  $P_{i,j}$  be the Markov transition matrix for a Markov chain on a finite state space
$S$  with elements  $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}$ .
Suppose that  $\sigma$  is a probability density on  $S$  that is invariant under this transition function:
$\sigma_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}P_{i,j}$  for all  $i$ . The transition matrix satisfies the detailed balance condition with respect to  $\sigma$  in case
(2.1)
$\sigma_{i}P_{i,j}=\sigma_{j}P_{j,i}\qquad{\rm for\ all}\ i,j\ .$
Let  $X_{n}$  be the Markov process started from the initial distribution  $\sigma$ , so that the process is stationary.
Let  ${\rm Pr}$  be measure on the path space of the process. Then (2.1) is equivalent to
${\rm Pr}\{X_{n}=i,X_{n+1}=j\}={\rm Pr}\{X_{n}=j,X_{n+1}=i\}\qquad{\rm for\ all}\ i,j\ {\rm and\ all}\ n\ .$
In other words,  $(X_{n},X_{n+1})$  has the same joint distribution as  $(X_{n+1},X_{n})$ , so that (2.1) characterizes time reversal invariance.
There is another characterization of (2.1) in terms of self-adjointness: The matrix  $P$  is self-adjoint on  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$  equipped with the inner product
(2.2)
$\langle f,g\rangle_{\sigma}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{k}\overline{f_{k}}g_{k}\ ,$
if and only if (2.1) is satisfied.
There are a number of different ways one might generalize the inner product (2.2) to
the quantum setting, and these give different notions of self-adjointness.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  be a QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$ .
A state  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$  is invariant under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$  in case  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma$  for all  $t\geq 0$ , or equivalently,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\sigma=0$ .
These conditions are equivalent to  ${\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(A)]={\rm Tr}[\sigma A]$  for all  $t>0$  and all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ , or equivalently,  ${\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A)]=0$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .
2.1 DEFINITION (Compatible inner product).
An inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$  is compatible with  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$
in case for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
${\rm Tr}[\sigma A]=\langle{{\bf 1}},A\rangle$ .
If a quantum Markov semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is self-adjoint with respect to an inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$  that is compatible with  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , then for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
${\rm Tr}[\sigma A]=\langle{{\bf 1}},A\rangle=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}{{\bf 1}},A\rangle=\langle{{\bf 1}},{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A\rangle={\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A]\ ,$
and thus  $\sigma$  is invariant under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$ .
2.2 DEFINITION.
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  be a non-degenerate density matrix.
For each  $s\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , and each  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ , define
(2.3)
$\langle A,B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[(\sigma^{(1-s)/2}A\sigma^{s/2})^{*}(\sigma^{(1-s)/2}B\sigma^{s/2})]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}A^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B]\ .$
Evidently each of these inner products is compatible with  $\sigma$ .
At  $s=1$ , this is the GNS inner product associated to the state  $\varphi(A)={\rm Tr}[\sigma A]$ .
The value  $s=1/2$  is also special;
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}$  is called the KMS inner product. A number of its properties are developed in [61].
The inner products in (2.3) can be written as
(2.4)
$\langle A,B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}^{1-s}B\sigma]\ .$
More generally, given any function  $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ , define
(2.5)
$\langle A,B\rangle_{f}={\rm Tr}[A^{*}f(\Delta_{\sigma})B\sigma]\ .$
Note that  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1}$  is the  $\sigma$ -GNS inner product whether  $1$  is interpreted as a number, as in (2.4), or as the constant function  $f(t)=1$ , as in (2.5).
Let  $R_{A}$  denote right multiplication by  $A$ , and define  $\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}=R_{\sigma}\circ f(\Delta_{\sigma})$ .
Then another way to write (2.5) is  $\langle A,B\rangle_{f}={\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}B]$ .
For all linear operators  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}B\rangle_{f}=\langle[\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}]^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}(\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}A),B\rangle_{f}\ .$
It follows immediately that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  if and only if
$\displaystyle\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}\circ{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\circ\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}\ .$
2.3 Remark.
For  $f(t)=t^{s}$ ,
the adjoint  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}$  of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with respect to the inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  is
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}B=\sigma^{s-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s})\sigma^{-s}\ .$
For  $s=1/2$ , this reduces to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}B=\sigma^{-1/2}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1/2}B\sigma^{1/2})\sigma^{-1/2}$ . Since
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}$  is positivity preserving if and only if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is positivity preserving, it is evident that for  $s=1/2$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}$  is positivity preserving if and only if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is positivity preserving. However, for other values of  $s$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}$  need not be positivity preserving when  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is. This is one feature that sets the KMS inner product
apart from the inner products
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  for other values of  $s$ .
In [70, Definition 16], detailed balance is defined in terms of self-adjointness with respect to
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$ , yielding a number of a priori different notions of detailed balance
depending on the choice of  $f$ .
The example following Proposition 18 in [70] shows that different choices of  $f$  can yield distinct classes of self-adjoint operators, and hence distinct notions of detailed balance.
Specifically, it is shown in [70] that self-adjointness with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}$  is not the same as self-adjointness with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  where  $f(t)=(1+t)/2$ , corresponding to the
Bures metric, as discussed in [70].
The authors of [70] conclude: “The family of quantum detailed balance conditions is therefore much richer than the classical counterpart”.
However, it turns out that self-adjointness with respect to the GNS inner product, or indeed with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  for any  $s\neq 1/2$  implies self-adjointness with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  for all  $f$ .
The argument leading to this conclusion, for which we have found no reference, is simple and will prove useful.
The following is a simple variant on the well-known KMS symmetry condition:
2.4 LEMMA.
For  $s\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , let  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  be the inner product defined in (2.3).
Then for all  $t\in{\mathbb{R}}$  and all  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
(2.6)
$\langle\alpha_{it}(A),B\rangle_{s}=\langle A,B\rangle_{s-t}=\langle A,\alpha_{it}(B)\rangle_{s}\ .$
In particular,  $\alpha_{it}$  is self-adjoint with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$ .
Proof.
Using the definitions we obtain
$\displaystyle\langle\alpha_{it}(A),B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}(\sigma^{t}A\sigma^{-t})^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s-t}A^{*}\sigma^{1-s+t}B]=\langle A,B\rangle_{s-t}=\langle A,\alpha_{it}(B)\rangle_{s}\ ,$
which is the desired identity ∎
The following lemma is a result of Alicki [5] for  $s=1$ , and the generalization to  $s\in[0,1]$ ,  $s\neq 1/2$ , can be found in [26, Propositon 8.1]. The following short proof, a simple adaptation of Alicki’s argument, is included for the reader’s convenience.
2.5 LEMMA.
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  be a non-degenerate density matrix, and let  $s\in[0,1]$ ,  $s\neq 1/2$ .
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  be any operator on  $\mathcal{A}$  that is self-adjoint with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  and also preserves self-adjointness.
Then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with  $\alpha_{t}$ , for all  $t$ , real and complex.
Proof.
For any  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\alpha_{i(2s-1)}(A),B\rangle_{s}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(\sigma^{2s-1}A\sigma^{1-2s}))^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}(\sigma^{2s-1}A\sigma^{1-2s})^{*}\sigma^{1-s}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B)]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{1-s}A^{*}\sigma^{s}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B)]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B^{*}))^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A^{*}]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}B\sigma^{1-s}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A^{*})]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{1-s}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A))^{*}\sigma^{s}B]=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),B\rangle_{1-s}$
Since  $s-(2s-1)=1-s$ , (2.6) yields  $\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),B\rangle_{1-s}=\langle\alpha_{i(2s-1)}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)),B\rangle_{s}$ .
As  $B$  is arbitrary,  $\alpha_{i(2s-1)}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\alpha_{i(2s-1)}$ .
Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with  $\alpha_{i(2s-1)}$ , it commutes with every polynomial in the
positive self-adjoint operator  $\alpha_{i(2s-1)}=\Delta_{\sigma}^{2s-1}$ , and hence with
$f(\Delta_{\sigma}^{2s-1})$  for every function  $f$ .
In particular,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with  $\alpha_{t}$  for all  $t$ .
∎
2.6 Remark.
Davies [21] has studied a class of quantum Markov semigroups
that arise in a general model of an  $n$ -level quantum system coupled to an infinite heat bath.
He studied the weak-coupling limit and gave conditions under which the
weak-coupling limit produces a quantum Markov semigroup.
This procedure always yields a semigroup that commutes with the evolution given by
(1.2) where  $h$  is the internal Hamiltonian of the  $n$ -level system.
This is true whether or not the semigroup has a particular self-adjointness property.
In view of Davies’ result, it is natural to focus on quantum Markov semigroups that commute
with the modular operator associated to their invariant states.
2.7 Remark.
The condition that the generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  of a quantum Markov semigroup
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  commutes with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  imposes strong restrictions on the structure of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ .
Consider the case  $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}_{2}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  have two distinct eigenvalues  $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0$ .
Let  $\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$  be an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathbb{C}}^{2}$  consisting of eigenvectors of
$\sigma$ :  $\sigma\eta_{j}=\lambda_{j}\eta_{j}$  for  $j=1,2$ .
Then  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  has three distinct eigenvalues  $1$ ,
$\lambda_{1}/\lambda_{2}$  and  $\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}$ .
The latter two eigenvalues have one-dimensional eigenspaces spanned by  $|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|$  and  $|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|$  respectively.
If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  commutes with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ , then  $|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|$  and  $|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|$  must be eigenvectors of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with eigenvalues, say,  $\nu$  and  $\tilde{\nu}$ .
Since  $A:=|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|+|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|$  is self-adjoint and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is self-adjointness preserving, it follows that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A)=\nu|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|+\tilde{\nu}|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|$  is self-adjoint, which implies that  $\tilde{\nu}=\nu$ .
Moreover, since both  $A$  and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A)=\nu A$  are self-adjoint, it follows that  $\nu$  is real.
Thus  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  has at most  $3$  eigenvalues  $1$ ,  $\mu$  and  $\nu$ , and  $\nu$  has multiplicity  $2$  (or  $3$  in case  $\nu=\mu$ ). To summarize, it follows that
(2.7)
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|)=\nu|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|\quad{\rm and}\quad{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|)=\nu|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|\quad\text{with }\nu\in{\mathbb{R}}\ .$
From here it is not hard to see that the value  $s=1/2$  is genuinely exceptional in Lemma 2.5.
Suppose that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the  $\sigma$ -KMS inner product
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}$  for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , where  $\sigma$  has distinct eigenvalues and  $\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$  is an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathbb{C}}^{2}$  consisting of eigenvectors of  $\sigma$ .
It follows from the discussion above that if (2.7) is violated,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  does not commute with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
There are many such operators  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{2}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
An explicit construction is given in Appendix B.
2.8 LEMMA.
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  be a non-degenerate density matrix.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  be any operator on  $\mathcal{A}$  such that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\alpha_{t}=\alpha_{t}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  for all  $t$ , or equivalently,  $\Delta_{\sigma}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  for some function  $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ , then the same holds for every function  $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ .
Proof.
Suppose that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  for some function  $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ . Let  $g:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$  be arbitrary, and write  $h=g/f$ . Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ , it also commutes with  $h(\Delta_{\sigma})$ . Thus, for all  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B)\rangle_{g}$
$\displaystyle={\rm Tr}[\sigma A^{*}g(\Delta_{\sigma}){\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B)]={\rm Tr}[\sigma A^{*}f(\Delta_{\sigma}){\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}h(\Delta_{\sigma})B]=\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}h(\Delta_{\sigma})B\rangle_{f}$
$\displaystyle=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),h(\Delta_{\sigma})B\rangle_{f}={\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)^{*}f(\Delta_{\sigma})h(\Delta_{\sigma})B]=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),B\rangle_{g}\ ,$
which is the desired result.
∎
We summarize some immediate consequences of the last lemmas in a theorem:
2.9 THEOREM.
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  be a non-degenerate density matrix, and let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  be any operator on  $\mathcal{A}$ . Then:
(1) If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the GNS inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1}$ ,
and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*}=({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with the modular automorphism group of  $\sigma$  and moreover,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  for all
$f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ .
(2) If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with the modular automorphism group of  $\sigma$ , and if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}$  for some  $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ , then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{g}$  for all  $g:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ .
This brings us to the definition of detailed balance, which is one the various definitions that may be found in the physical literature.
2.10 DEFINITION (Detailed balance).
A QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  satisfies the detailed balance condition with respect to
$\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$  in case for each  $t>0$ ,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is self-adjoint in the  $\sigma$ -GNS inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1}$ .
In this case  $\sigma$  is invariant under
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$ , and we say that the QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC.
2.11 Remark.
Every QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  is self-adjointness preserving:  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A^{*}=({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A)^{*}$ .
Thus, when  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC, it follows from Theorem 2.9 that
(2.8)
$\alpha_{t^{\prime}}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(A))={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(\alpha_{t^{\prime}}(A))$
for all  $t,t^{\prime}$  and all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .
This crucial observation is due to Alicki [5], and it means that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  commutes with the time-translation governed by the Hamiltonian  $h$  corresponding to the state
$\sigma$ . The condition (2.8) may therefore be viewed as a quantum analog of time-translation
invariance or stationarity.
Theorem 2.9 asserts that in the presence of detailed balance,
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is self-adjoint with respect to a wide variety of inner products and also that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  commutes with the modular group.
Moreover, under the condition that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  commutes with the modular group, self-adjointness
with respect to any member of this wide family of inner products implies self-adjointness
with respect to all of them. This is important in what follows.
The inner products defined just above include a number of inner products that arise
naturally in the theory of operator algebras and mathematical physics.
One that will be especially useful here is the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori inner product:
$\langle A,B\rangle_{{\rm BKM}}=\int_{0}^{1}{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{1-s}A^{*}\sigma^{s}B]{\rm d}s=\int_{0}^{1}{\rm Tr}[\sigma A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}B]{\rm d}s=\langle A,B\rangle_{f_{0}}\ ,$
where
$f_{0}(t)=\int_{0}^{1}t^{s}{\rm d}s=\frac{t-1}{\log t}\ .$
The BKM inner product arises naturally in statistical mechanics and our work here as follows:
For a self-adjoint operator  $h$  on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space  $\mathcal{H}$ , and  $\beta>0$ ,
define the Gibbs state  $\sigma_{\beta}$  by
$\sigma_{\beta}=\frac{1}{{\rm Tr}[e^{-\beta h}]}e^{-\beta h}\ .$
The free energy is the functional  $\mathcal{F}(\beta,h)=\beta^{-1}\log({\rm Tr}[e^{-\beta h}])$ . A simple calculation using Duhamel’s formula shows that for any self-adjoint  $A$ ,
$\frac{{\rm d}^{2}}{{\rm d}s^{2}}\mathcal{F}(\beta,h+sA)\bigg|_{s=0}=\beta\left[\langle A,A\rangle_{{\rm BKM}}-({\rm Tr}[\sigma_{\beta}A])^{2}\right]\ .$
In particular, up to a factor of  $\beta$ ,  $\langle A,A\rangle_{{\rm BKM}}$  arises as the restriction of the Hessian of  $\mathcal{F}$  to the space of self-adjoint matrices  $A$  satisfying  ${\rm Tr}[\sigma_{\beta}A]=0$ .
It is well known that for fixed  $\beta$ , the function  $h\mapsto\mathcal{F}(\beta,h)$  is the Legendre transform of the von Neumann entropy  $S(\rho)$  on the set of density matrices.
Since the gradients and Hessians of conjugate convex functions are inverse to one another, the Hessian of the free energy is the inverse of Hessian of the entropy; a fact that explains why the BKM inner product will arise naturally in the study of gradient flows of the relative entropy.
3. Generators of quantum Markov semigroups satisfying detailed balance
Since a QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for some  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$
has a generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  that commutes with the modular operator  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ , and since
$\Delta_{\sigma}$  is positive with respect to the GNS inner product,  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  can be simultaneously diagonalized. In the case  $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , the diagonalization of
$\Delta_{\sigma}$  reduces immediately to the diagonalization of  $\sigma$ : Let  $\sigma=e^{-h}$  be a density matrix
on  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ . Let  $\{\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{n}\}$  be an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$  consisting of eigenvectors of  $h=-\log\sigma$ :
$h\eta_{j}=\lambda_{j}\eta_{j}$ . For  $\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\in\{(i,j)\ :1\leq i,j\leq n\}$ , define numbers
$\omega_{\alpha}$  (called the Bohr frequencies) by
(3.1)
$\omega_{\alpha}=\lambda_{\alpha_{1}}-\lambda_{\alpha_{2}}\ ,$
and rank-one operators  $F_{\alpha}$  given by
$F_{\alpha}=|\eta_{\alpha_{1}}\rangle\langle\eta_{\alpha_{2}}|$
where, using a standard physics notation, for  $\eta,\xi\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ ,  $|\eta\rangle\langle\xi|$  is the rank-one operator sending  $\zeta$  to  $\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle_{{\mathbb{C}}^{n}}\eta$ .
Evidently
(3.2)
$\Delta_{\sigma}F_{\alpha}=e^{-\omega_{\alpha}}F_{\alpha}\qquad{\rm and}\qquad F_{\alpha}^{*}=F_{\alpha^{\prime}}\quad{\rm where}\quad\alpha^{\prime}=(\alpha_{2},\alpha_{1})\ .$
Alicki [5] exploited such a construction to show that for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$
with non-degenerate spectrum (in the sense that each eigenvalue of  $\sigma$  is simple), the generator
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  of a quantum Markov semigroup on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that satisfies the
$\sigma$ -DBC (so that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  commutes with  $\Delta_{\sigma})$  has the form described in (3.3) below; see
[5, Theorem 3].
(Alicki actually considered the more general case that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is normal with respect to the
$\sigma$ -GNS inner product.
His formula reduces to (3.3) when  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is self-adjoint.)
The hypothesis that  $\sigma$  has non-degenerate spectrum turns out to unnecessary.
In the context of full matrix algebras this has been shown in
[42] for the alternate canonical form given in [5, Theorem 3].
It is possible to give a simple and self-contained proof of Alicki’s Theorem in a somewhat more general setting. This is done in Appendix A; the theorem proved there is:
3.1 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be a QMS on a unital  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra
$\mathcal{A}$  of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ . Suppose that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for
$\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$  and that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  has an extension  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  to a QMS on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Regard the modular operator  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  as an operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  and
let  $\tau$  denote the normalized trace on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Then the generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  has the form
(3.3)
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\Big(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}V_{j}^{*}[A,V_{j}]+e^{\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j},A]V_{j}^{*}\Big)$
(3.4)
$\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\Big(V_{j}^{*}[A,V_{j}]+[V_{j}^{*},A]V_{j}\Big)$
where  $\omega_{j}\in{\mathbb{R}}$  for all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ , and  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  is a set in
$\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  with the properties:
(i)  $\tau[V_{j}^{*}V_{k}]=\delta_{j,k}$  for all  $j,k\in{\mathcal{J}}$ .
(ii)  $\tau[V_{j}]=0$  for all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ .
(iii)  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}=\{V_{j}^{*}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$ .
(iv)  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  consists of eigenvectors of the modular operator  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  with
(3.5)
$\Delta_{\sigma}V_{j}=e^{-\omega_{j}}V_{j}\ .$
Conversely, given any  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ , and any set  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  satisfying (iii) and (iv) for some  $\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}$ , the operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  given by (3.3) is the generator of a QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC.
3.2 Remark.
The eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  with eigenvalues other than  $1$  cannot be self-adjoint on account of (1.3). However, when  $\sigma$  is the normalized trace,  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  is the identity, so that each  $V_{j}$  is an eigenvector of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  with eigenvalue  $1$ , thus  $\omega_{j}=0$ .
It is then possible to take each  $V_{j}$  to be self-adjoint, so that (3.4) reduces to
(3.6)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}[V_{j},[V_{j},A]]\ .$
This formulation arises naturally in various applications, as we shall see in Section 6.
3.3 Remark.
By Theorem 3.1, the Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is given by
(3.7)
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\Big(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j}\rho,V_{j}^{*}]+e^{\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j}^{*},\rho V_{j}]\Big)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\Big([V_{j}\rho,V_{j}^{*}]+[V_{j},\rho V_{j}^{*}]\Big)\ .$
3.4 Remark.
Note that the operators in  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  need not belong to  $\mathcal{A}$  itself. The Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup in the Clifford algebra with an odd number of generators provides an example in which they
do not, as we discuss shortly.
3.5 Remark.
By properties (i) and (ii),
the index set  ${\mathcal{J}}$  has cardinality
$|{\mathcal{J}}|$  no greater than  $n^{2}-1$ . While in general the set  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  is not uniquely determined, the proof in the appendix shows that  $|{\mathcal{J}}|$  is uniquely determined.
Moreover, if  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $\{\tilde{V}_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  are two such sets, there is an  $|{\mathcal{J}}|\times|{\mathcal{J}}|$  unitary matrix  $U_{j,k}$  such that for all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ ,  ${\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{j}=\sum_{k\in{\mathcal{J}}}U_{j,k}V_{k}}$ ,
and such that unless  $\tilde{\omega}_{k}=\omega_{j}$ ,  $U_{k,j}=0$ .
Thus, in a strong sense, the sets  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$
are canonically associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ . (Indeed, since  $\Delta_{\sigma}V_{j}=e^{-\omega_{j}}V_{j}$ , the numbers
$\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  are fixed once  $\sigma$  and the set  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  is fixed.)
4. Restriction to commutative subalgebras
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be a unital  $C^{*}$ -algebra, and let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ . Let  $A_{1},A_{2}$  be eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ :  $\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{j})=\lambda_{j}A_{j}$ ,  $j=1,2$ .
Then  $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0$ , and since the modular operator is an automorphism,
$\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{1}A_{2})=\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{1})\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{2})=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}A_{1}A_{2}\ .$
That is, the product of eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  is again an eigenvector of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ , and moreover, the eigenspace of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  for the eigenvalue  $1$  is an algebra.
In fact, by (1.3) it is a  $*$ -algebra, and it consists exactly of those elements  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  that commute with  $\sigma$ . Clearly,  $\sigma$  itself always belongs to  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$ .
4.1 DEFINITION (Modular subalgebra).
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be a unital  $C^{*}$ -algebra, and let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ .
The  $\sigma$ -modular subalgebra of  $\mathcal{A}$ , denoted  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$ , is the  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra of  $\mathcal{A}$  consisting of the eigenspace of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  with eigenvalue  $1$ .
Of course if  $\sigma={{\bf 1}}$ ,  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  is the identity on  $\mathcal{A}$ , and then  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}=\mathcal{A}$ .
On the other hand, suppose that  $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  and let  $\{\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{n}\}$  be an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$  consisting of eigenvectors of  $\sigma$  with  $\sigma\eta_{j}=e^{-\lambda_{j}}\eta_{j}$  for  $j=1,\dots,n$ .
Then for each  $1\leq i,j\leq n$ ,  $|\eta_{i}\rangle\langle\eta_{j}|$  is an eigenvector of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  with eigenvalue  $e^{\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{i}}$ .
If the numbers  $\{\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{m}\}$ , which are the eigenvalues of the modular generator  $h$ , are all distinct, then the eigenspace of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  for the eigenvalue  $1$  is exactly the span of the set  $\{|\eta_{j}\rangle\langle\eta_{j}|\}_{j=1}^{n}$  [5].
In this case  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$  is an  $n$ -dimensional commutative  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra of  $\mathcal{A}$ .
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be an ergodic QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$ , and let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  be its unique invariant state.
Suppose that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC.
Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  and  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  commute by Theorem 2.9, the  $\sigma$ -modular subalgebra  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$  of  $\mathcal{A}$  is invariant under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  (and under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$  as well).
In this case, let  ${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.37502pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.94775pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.94775pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.3988pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=4.50006pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}}_{t}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$  denote the restriction of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  to  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$ .
If  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$  is commutative, then  ${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.37502pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.94775pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.94775pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.3988pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=4.50006pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}}_{t}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$  is an ergodic QMS on a commutative subalgebra of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , which may be identified with the transition semigroup of a classical Markov chain.
This happens whenever each eigenvalue of  $\sigma$  is simple [5].
Therefore, consider a QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC.
Suppose that  $\mathcal{A}$  is a unital commutative  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that is invariant under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$ .
If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is ergodic, it follows using the self-adjointness of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1}$ , that for any  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ ,  $\sigma=\lim_{t\to\infty}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho$ , and hence  $\sigma\in\mathcal{A}$ .
In our finite-dimensional setting, there exists a finite set  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}$  of minimal projections in  $\mathcal{A}$  such that  $\sum_{k=1}^{m}E_{k}={{\bf 1}}$ .
Consequently,  $E_{j}E_{k}=0$  for all  $j\neq k$ , and  $\mathcal{A}$  is the span of  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}$ : For all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  we have
(4.1)
$A=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{a_{k}}{{\rm Tr}[E_{k}]}E_{k}\quad{\rm where}\quad a_{k}={\rm Tr}[E_{k}A]\ .$
Define an  $m\times m$  matrix  $Q$  by
(4.2)
$Q_{k,\ell}=\frac{1}{{\rm Tr}[E_{k}]}{\rm Tr}[E_{k}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}E_{\ell}]\ .$
A vector  $\vec{\rho}=(\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{m})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$  is a probability vector in case  $\rho_{k}\geq 0$  for all  $k$ , and  $\sum_{k=1}^{m}\rho_{k}=1$ .
4.2 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be an ergodic QMS on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for its invariant state  $\sigma$ .
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be a unital commutative  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that is invariant under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$ .
Let  $\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\}$  be a set of minimal projections in  $\mathcal{A}$  such that  $\sum_{k=1}^{m}E_{k}={{\bf 1}}$ .
The  $m\times m$  matrix  $Q$  defined by (4.2) specifies an ergodic continuous-time Markov chain on  $\{1,\dots,m\}$  with jump rates  $Q_{k,\ell}$  from  $k$  to  $\ell$ . The corresponding forward equation, governing the evolution of site occupation probabilities is
(4.3)
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\rho_{\ell}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\big(\rho_{k}(t)Q_{k,\ell}-\rho_{\ell}(t)Q_{\ell,k}\big)\ .$
A time-dependent probability vector  $\vec{\rho}(t)$  satisfies (4.3) if and only if the time-dependent state  $\rho(t)$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  given by
(4.4)
$\rho(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\rho_{k}(t)}{{\rm Tr}[E_{k}]}E_{k}$
satisfies  $\displaystyle{\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\rho(t)={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho(t)}$ . Moreover, the probability vector  $\vec{\sigma}$  given by  $\sigma_{k}={\rm Tr}[\sigma E_{k}]$  for  $k=1,\dots,m$  is the unique invariant probability vector for the Markov chain, and the classical detailed balance condition
(4.5)
$\sigma_{k}Q_{k,\ell}=\sigma_{\ell}Q_{\ell,k}$
is satisfied.
Proof.
We first show that the matrix  $Q$  satisfies  $\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}Q_{k,\ell}=0$  and that  $Q_{k,\ell}\geq 0$  for all  $k\neq\ell$ , which makes it a transition rate matrix.
Since  $0={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}E_{\ell}$ , we have  $\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}Q_{k,\ell}=0$ .
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be given in the form (3.4).
Then for  $k\neq\ell$ , simple computations yield
${\rm Tr}[E_{k}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}E_{\ell}]=2\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}e^{-\omega_{j}/2}{\rm Tr}[E_{k}V_{j}^{*}E_{\ell}V_{j}].$
Since  $E_{k}$  and  $V_{j}^{*}E_{\ell}V_{j}$  are positive,  ${\rm Tr}[E_{k}V_{j}^{*}E_{\ell}V_{j}]\geq 0$ , showing that  $Q_{k,\ell}\geq 0$  for all  $k\neq\ell$ .
Now suppose that  $a_{k}:=\sum_{\ell\neq k}Q_{k,\ell}=0$ .
Then from the definition,  ${\rm Tr}[{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(E_{k})E_{\ell}]={\rm Tr}[E_{k}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(E_{\ell})]=0$  for all  $k\neq\ell$ , and then, since  $\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}Q_{k,\ell}=0$ , also  ${\rm Tr}[{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(E_{k})E_{k}]=0$ .
It would follow that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(E_{k})=0$ .
Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is ergodic, this is impossible unless  $\mathcal{A}$  is spanned by  ${{\bf 1}}$ , a trivial case.
Hence we may proceed assuming that  $a_{k}>0$  for all  $k$ .
Define the matrix  $P_{k,\ell}$  by
$\displaystyle{P_{k,\ell}=\begin{cases}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{a_{k}}Q_{k,\ell}}&\ell\neq k\\
0&\ell=k\end{cases}}\ .$
Evidently  $P$  is an  $m\times m$  stochastic matrix. Define the  $m\times m$  matrix  $M$  by
$M_{k,\ell}=a_{k}\delta_{k,\ell}$ .
Then  $Q=M(P-{{\bf 1}}_{m})$  where  ${{\bf 1}}_{m}$  is the  $m\times m$  identity matrix. The equation
${\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\vec{\rho}(t)=Q^{\dagger}\vec{\rho}(t)}$
is solved in terms of the initial data
$\vec{\rho}_{0}$  by  $\vec{\rho}(t)=e^{tQ^{\dagger}}\vec{\rho}_{0}$ ,
and it gives the site occupation probabilities for a continuous time Markov chain in which the jump rate for leaving site  $k$  is  $a_{k}$ , and when such a jump occurs, the probability that site  $\ell$  is the new site occupied is given by  $P_{k,\ell}$ .
The equation
${\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\vec{\rho}(t)=Q^{\dagger}\vec{\rho}(t)}$  can be written as
(4.6)
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\rho_{\ell}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\rho_{k}(t)Q_{k,\ell}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\big(\rho_{k}(t)Q_{k,\ell}-\rho_{\ell}(t)Q_{\ell,k}\big)\ ,$
where the second equality follows from the first and the fact that  $Q_{\ell,\ell}=-\sum_{k\neq\ell}Q_{\ell,k}$ .
This gives us (4.3).
To show that this Markov chain satisfies the classical detailed balance condition (4.5),
observe that  $\sigma E_{k}=\sigma_{k}({\rm Tr}[E_{k}])^{-1}E_{k}=E_{k}\sigma$  by (4.1), and therefore
$\displaystyle\sigma_{k}Q_{k,\ell}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{k}}{{\rm Tr}[E_{k}]}{\rm Tr}[E_{k}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(E_{\ell})]={\rm Tr}[\sigma E_{k}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(E_{\ell})]={\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(E_{k})E_{\ell}]$
$\displaystyle={\rm Tr}[E_{\ell}\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(E_{k})]=\frac{\sigma_{\ell}}{{\rm Tr}[E_{\ell}]}{\rm Tr}[E_{\ell}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(E_{k})]=\sigma_{\ell}Q_{\ell,k}\ ,$
where the third equality holds since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is self-adjoint for the  $\sigma$ -GNS inner product. It follows immediately from (4.6) that  $\vec{\sigma}$  is invariant.
Finally, it is easy to check using the definition of the matrix  $Q$  in terms of the generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  that  $\vec{\rho}(t)$  satisfies (4.6) if and only if
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\rho(t)={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho(t)$ .
Ergodicity of the Markov chain  ${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.37502pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.94775pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.94775pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.3988pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=4.50006pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}}_{t}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$  now follows from the ergodicity of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ .
∎
5. Dirichlet form representation associated to a quantum Markov generator
Let  $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(X,{\mathord{\mathscr{B}}},\mu)$  be the space of square integrable real-valued functions on some probability space  $(X,{\mathord{\mathscr{B}}},\mu)$ .
A closed and densely defined, symmetric non-negative bilinear form  $\mathcal{E}$  on  $\mathcal{H}$  defines a non-negative unbounded operator  $-A$  through  $\mathcal{E}(f,g)=-\langle f,Ag\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$ . A special case ( $\mu$  is a probability measure) of a theorem of
Beurling and Deny [8, 9] states that  $P_{t}=e^{tA}$  is a Markov semigroup if and only if for all  $f\in\mathcal{H}$ ,
$\mathcal{E}(\widehat{f},\widehat{f})\leq\mathcal{E}(f,f)$  where  $\widehat{f}$  denotes the projection of  $f$  onto the closed convex set  $\{g\in\mathcal{H}\ :\ 0\leq g\leq 1\ {\rm a.e.}\}$ .
A powerful non-commutative extension of this theory has been developed starting with the early work of Gross [32, 33], and continuing with [4, 16, 17, 19, 22, 30]. We shall not need the whole theory at present, but the Dirichlet form representation of the generator of a QMS will be useful to us.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be a QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for some  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ .
The generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  can then be written in the canonical form specified in (3.4) of Theorem 3.1.
Throughout the rest of this section we fix such a generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ , and the sets  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $\{\omega_{j}\}$  that specify  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  in the form (3.4).
Define operators  $\partial_{j}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  by
$\partial_{j}A=[V_{j},A]\quad{\rm so\ that}\quad\partial_{j}^{\dagger}A=[V_{j}^{*},A]\ .$
The operators  $\partial_{j}$  are derivations, and we may consider them as non-commutative analogs of partial derivatives associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ . With respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product, we may then form non-commutative analogs of the gradient, divergence and Laplacian associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ . We begin with the Laplacian:
Given the set  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$ , we define an operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  by
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\partial_{j}A=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}[V_{j}^{*},[V_{j},A]]\ .$
Evidently  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}^{\dagger}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$ , and we may write
${\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}(V_{j}^{*}[A,V_{j}]+[V_{j},A]V_{j}^{*})}$ .
Thus, by Theorem 3.1,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  is the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}}$  satisfying detailed balance with respect to  $\tau$ .
We call this semigroup the heat semigroup associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ , and the operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  the Laplace operator associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ .
We define the Hilbert space  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  by
${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}=\bigoplus_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{(j)}\ ,$
where each  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{(j)}$  is a copy of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ .
For  ${\bf A}\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ , let  $A_{j}$  denote the component of  ${\bf A}$  in  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{(j)}$ . Thus, picking some linear ordering of  ${\mathcal{J}}$ , we can write
${\bf A}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ .$
We equip  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  with the usual inner product
${\langle{\bf A},{\bf B}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j},B_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}}$ .
Define an operator
$\nabla:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  by
$\nabla A=(\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}A)\ .$
Thinking of elements of  $\mathcal{A}$  as non-commutative analogs of functions on a manifold, we may think of
${\bf A}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})$  as a vector field. This point of view will be justified in the next section.
We define the operator  $\dive:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  by
$\dive{\bf A}=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}A_{j}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}[A_{j},V_{j}^{*}]\ .$
Note that  $\dive$  is minus the adjoint of the map  $\nabla:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$ , so that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  is negative semi-definite.
With these definitions,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}=\dive\circ\nabla$ . We call  $\nabla$  the non-commutative gradient associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ , and  $\dive$  the non-commutative divergence associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ .
5.1 Remark.
In this finite-dimensional setting, by elementary linear algebra,
(5.1)
$\big({\rm Null}(\dive)\big)^{\perp}={\rm Ran}(\nabla)\ .$
In the terminology introduced above, elements of  ${\rm Null}(\dive)$  are divergence free vector fields.
Then (5.1) says that a vector field  ${\bf A}$  is a gradient if and only if it is orthogonal in  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  to every divergence free vector field.
The differential structure introduced above allows us to write the generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  of a QMS in terms of a non-commutative Dirichlet form.
5.2 LEMMA.
For all  $s\in[0,1]$ , all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ , and all  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$  we have
(5.2)
$\langle\partial_{j}B,A\rangle_{s}=\langle B,e^{s\omega_{j}}(e^{-\omega_{j}}V_{j}^{*}A-AV^{*}_{j})\rangle_{s}\ .$
Proof.
For any  $A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle\partial_{j}B,A\rangle_{s}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}(\partial_{j}B)^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}(V_{j}B-BV_{j})^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}B^{*}V_{j}^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A]-{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}V_{j}^{*}B^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}B^{*}\sigma^{1-s}\Delta_{\sigma}^{s-1}(V_{j}^{*})A]-{\rm Tr}[\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}(V_{j}^{*})\sigma^{s}B^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle e^{(s-1)\omega_{j}}{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}B^{*}\sigma^{1-s}V_{j}^{*}A]-e^{s\omega_{j}}{\rm Tr}[V_{j}^{*}\sigma^{s}B^{*}\sigma^{1-s}A]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\big\langle{B,e^{s\omega_{j}}(e^{-\omega_{j}}V_{j}^{*}A-AV_{j}^{*})}\big\rangle_{s}\ ,$
where in the fourth line we have used (3.5).
∎
It follows from (5.2) that for all  $s\in[0,1]$ , and all  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ ,
$e^{(1/2-s)\omega_{j}}\langle{\partial_{j}B,\partial_{j}A}\rangle_{s}=-\big\langle{B,e^{-\omega_{j}/2}V_{j}^{*}[A,V_{j}]+e^{\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j},A]V^{*}_{j}}\big\rangle_{s}\ .$
Using the expression for  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  given in (3.3), we obtain
${\mathcal{E}}_{s}(B,A)=-\langle{B,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A}\rangle_{s}\ ,\quad\text{ where }\quad{\mathcal{E}}_{s}(B,A):=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}e^{(1/2-s)\omega_{j}}\langle{\partial_{j}B,\partial_{j}A}\rangle_{s}\ .$
In particular, taking  $s=1/2$ , we see that
(5.3)
${\mathcal{E}}_{1/2}(B,A)=-\langle{B,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A}\rangle_{1/2}\ ,\quad\text{ where }\quad{\mathcal{E}}_{1/2}(B,A):=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\partial_{j}B,\partial_{j}A}\rangle_{1/2}\ ,$
which expresses  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  in terms of a Dirichlet form in the sense of [30, 16, 17].
As a simple consequence of the Dirichlet form representation, we state an ergodicity result.
Recall that a QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  is ergodic in case for each  $t>0$ , the  $1$ -eigenspace of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is spanned by the identity, or, what is the same thing, the  $0$ -eigenspace of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is spanned by the identity. We refer to [29] for an early study of ergodicity for quantum dynamical semigroups.
5.3 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ .
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be given in the form (3.4).
Then the commutant of  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  equals the null space of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ .
In particular,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is ergodic if and only if the commutant of  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  is spanned by the identity.
Proof.
Suppose that  $A$  belongs to the commutant of  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$ .
By definition, this means that  $\partial_{j}A=0$  for all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ , and therefore  $A\in{\rm Null}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}})$  by (3.3).
Conversely, if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=0$ , then by (5.3),
$0=-\langle{A,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A}\rangle_{1/2}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\partial_{j}A,\partial_{j}A}\rangle_{1/2}\ ,$
which is the case if and only if  $[V_{j},A]=0$  for all  $j$ . This means that  $A$  belongs to the commutant of  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$ .
∎
5.4 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be an ergodic QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ , and let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  be the associated Laplacian.
Then for given  $B\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ , the equation
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}X=B$
has a solution if and only if  $\tau[B]=0$ .
Consequently, when  $\tau[B]=0$ , there is a non-trivial affine subspace of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  consisting of elements  ${\bf A}$  for which  $\dive{\bf A}=B$ .
Proof.
Since  $\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=-\langle\nabla A,\nabla A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}}$ , we have  ${\rm Null}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0})={\rm Null}(\nabla)$ .
Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is ergodic, it follows from Theorem 5.3 that  ${\rm Null}(\nabla)$  is spanned by  ${{\bf 1}}$ . Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  is self-adjoint on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ , the assertion now follows from the Fredholm alternative.
∎
The following identity will be useful going forward.
5.5 LEMMA (Chain rule identity).
For all  $V\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ ,  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  and  $\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}$ ,
(5.4)
$\int_{0}^{1}e^{\omega(s-1/2)}R_{\rho}\Delta_{\rho}^{s}\Big(V\log(e^{-\omega/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega/2}\rho)V\Big)\>{\rm d}s=e^{-\omega/2}V\rho-e^{\omega/2}\rho V\ .$
Proof.
Define  $f(s)=e^{\omega(1/2-s)}\rho^{1-s}V\rho^{s}$ . The right side of (5.4) equals  $f(1)-f(0)$  and
$\displaystyle f^{\prime}(s)$
$\displaystyle=e^{\omega(1/2-s)}\rho^{1-s}\Big(-\omega V-\log(\rho)V+V\log(\rho)\Big)\rho^{s}$
$\displaystyle=e^{\omega(1/2-s)}\rho^{1-s}\Big(V\log(e^{-\omega/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega/2}\rho)V\Big)\rho^{s}\ .$
Thus the left side of (5.4) equals  $\int_{0}^{1}f^{\prime}(1-s)\>{\rm d}s$ , which yields the result.
∎
5.6 Remark.
Consider the function  $f_{\omega}$  defined by
(5.5)
$f_{\omega}(t):=\int_{0}^{1}e^{\omega(s-1/2)}t^{s}\>{\rm d}s=e^{\omega/2}\frac{t-e^{-\omega}}{\log t+\omega}\ .$
Then (5.4) can be formulated as
(5.6)
$R_{\rho}f_{\omega}(\Delta_{\rho})\Big(V\log(e^{-\omega/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega/2}\rho)V\Big)=e^{-\omega/2}V\rho-e^{\omega/2}\rho V\ .$
Notice that for  $\omega=0$ , (5.4) reduces to the commutator identity
(5.7)
$R_{\rho}f_{0}(\Delta_{\rho})([V,\log\rho])=[V,\rho]\ .$
This identity provides a quantum analog of the classical identity for smooth, strictly positive probability densities  $\rho(x)$  on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ :
(5.8)
$\rho(x)\nabla\log\rho(x)=\nabla\rho(x)\ .$
To see this, note that if  $A$  commutes with  $\rho$ ,  $f_{\omega}(\Delta_{\rho})A=A$
so that for each  $\omega$ , the operation  ${\displaystyle A\mapsto R_{\rho}f_{\omega}(\Delta_{\rho})A}$  is one of the
non-commutative interpretations of multiplication of  $A$  by  $\rho$ .
Now applying (5.7) with  $V=V_{j}$ , we have
$R_{\rho}f_{0}(\Delta_{\rho})(\partial_{j}\log\rho)=\partial_{j}\rho$
for each  $j$ , which yields a quantum analog of (5.8).
Lemma 5.5 and the previous remark motivate the following definition:
5.7 DEFINITION.
For  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and  $\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , define the operator  $[\rho]_{\omega}:\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\to\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  by
(5.9)
$[\rho]_{\omega}=R_{\rho}\circ f_{\omega}(\Delta_{\rho})$
For each  $\omega$ ,  $[\rho]_{\omega}$ , which is one of the non-commutative forms of multiplication by  $\rho$ , is evidently invertible, and its inverse,  $[\rho]_{\omega}^{-1}=(1/f_{\omega})(\Delta_{\rho})\circ R_{\rho^{-1}}$  may then be viewed as the corresponding non-commutative form of division by  $\rho$ .
We remark that  $[\rho]_{\omega}^{-1}$  is a kernel operator that can be used to define a monotone metric on density matrices in the sense of [62]. However, the Riemannian metric on density matrices that we introduce in this paper will be different.
5.8 LEMMA.
For all  $\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , the maps  $\rho\mapsto[\rho]_{\omega}$  and  $\rho\mapsto[\rho]_{\omega}^{-1}$  are  $C^{\infty}$  on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ . Furthermore, for all  $A$ ,
(5.10)
$([\rho]_{\omega}A)^{*}=[\rho]_{-\omega}A^{*}\quad{\rm and\ consequently}\quad([\rho]^{-1}_{\omega}A)^{*}=[\rho]^{-1}_{-\omega}A^{*}\ .$
Proof.
Recall the identities
(5.11)
$\int_{0}^{1}\lambda^{1-s}\mu^{s}\>{\rm d}s=\frac{\lambda-\mu}{\log\lambda-\log\mu}\quad{\rm and}\quad\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(t+\lambda)(t+\mu)}\>{\rm d}t=\frac{\log\lambda-\log\mu}{\lambda-\mu}\ ,$
which hold for  $\lambda,\mu>0$ .
By (5.5) and (5.9) we obtain
(5.12)
$\displaystyle[\rho]_{\omega}=R_{\rho}f_{\omega}(\Delta_{\rho})=\int_{0}^{1}e^{\omega(1/2-s)}L_{\rho}^{s}R_{\rho}^{1-s}\>{\rm d}s=\int_{0}^{1}(e^{-\omega/2}L_{\rho})^{s}(e^{\omega/2}R_{\rho})^{1-s}\>{\rm d}s\ ,$
and it follows from (5.11) that
$\displaystyle[\rho]_{\omega}^{-1}=\int_{0}^{\infty}(t+e^{-\omega/2}L_{\rho})^{-1}(t+e^{\omega/2}R_{\rho})^{-1}\>{\rm d}t\ .$
The fact that  $\rho\mapsto[\rho]_{\omega}^{-1}$  is  $C^{\infty}$  now follows immediately from the resolvent identity, and then the  $C^{\infty}$ -differentiability of  $\rho\mapsto[\rho]_{\omega}$  is clear. Moreover, (5.10) follows from (5.12).
∎
It is now a simple matter to write the quantum heat flow equation  $\partial\rho/\partial t={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}^{\dagger}\rho$
in a form that leads directly to its interpretation as gradient flow for the relative entropy with respect to the normalized trace:
For all  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}^{\dagger}\rho=\dive([\rho]_{0}\nabla\log\rho)\ ,$
where  $[\rho]_{0}$  is applied to each component of  $\nabla\log\rho$ .
As we show in the next section, it follows easily from this formula that there is a Riemannian metric on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , which is a natural analog of the  $2$ -Wasserstein metric, such that the quantum heat flow on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  associated to  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  is a gradient flow for the relative entropy of  $\rho$  with respect to the normalized trace  $\tau$ . For a comprehensive treatment of the theory of gradient flows with respect to the  $2$ -Wasserstein metric, see [6] and [73, Chapters 23-25].
In fact, the next lemma provides the means to extend this result to the general class of quantum Markov semigroups that satisfy detailed balance with respect to some non-degenerate state  $\sigma$ .
5.9 LEMMA.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the
$\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ . and let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be given in the form (3.4).
Then for all  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ ,
$\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)=V_{j}\log(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho)V_{j}\ .$
Proof.
By (3.5) we have  $\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}V_{j}=e^{-s\omega_{j}}V_{j}$ , and thus  $[V_{j},\log\sigma]=-\partial_{s}|_{s=0}\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}V_{j}=\omega_{j}V_{j}$ .
It follows that
$\displaystyle\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)=[V_{j},\log\rho]-\omega_{j}V_{j}=V_{j}\log(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho)V_{j}\ ,$
which is the desired identity.
∎
5.10 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ , and let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be given in the form (3.4). Then, for all  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ ,
$-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\Big)\ .$
Proof.
Using Lemma 5.9 and (5.6) we obtain
$\displaystyle\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\Big)$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\Big(V_{j}\log(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho)V_{j}\Big)\Big)$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}V_{j}\rho-e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho V_{j}\Big)$
$\displaystyle=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\Big(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j}\rho,V_{j}^{*}]+e^{\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j}^{*},\rho V_{j}]\Big)=-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho\ ,$
where the final identity follows from (3.7).
∎
6. Examples
6.1. The infinite-temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup
As Segal emphasized [66], the Fermion number operator for  $n$  degrees of freedom can be represented in terms of the generators of a Clifford algebra. This permits the semigroup it generates to be realized as a QMS, a fact that was effectively exploited by Gross [32, 33] using Segal’s non-commutative integration theory [65, 67].
Let  $\{Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}\}$  be self-adjoint operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space satisfying the canonical anti-commutation relations (CAR):
$\displaystyle Q_{j}Q_{k}+Q_{k}Q_{j}=2\delta_{jk}{{\bf 1}}\;.$
The Clifford algebra  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  is the  $2^{n}$ -dimensional algebra generated by  $\{Q_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}$ .
Let  $\Gamma:\mathfrak{C}^{n}\to\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  be the principle automorphism on  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$ , i.e., the unique algebra
isomorphism satisfying  $\Gamma(Q_{j})=-Q_{j}$  for all  $j$ . The product of all of the generators
$Q_{1}Q_{2}\cdots Q_{n}$  (in some order) is evidently unitary,
and the CAR imply that it commutes with each  $Q_{j}$  if  $n$  is odd, and anti-commutes with each  $Q_{j}$  if  $n$  is even.
Hence when  $n$  is odd, the center of  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  is non-trivial and  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  is not a factor.
In the even case  $n=2m$ , form the  $m$  self-adjoint unitary operators  $iQ_{2j-1}Q_{2j}$ ,  $j=1,\dots n$ .
These all commute with one another, and we define
$W=i^{m}Q_{1}Q_{2}\cdots Q_{2m}\ .$
Evidently  $W\in\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  is unitary and self-adjoint, and since  $W$  anti-commutes with each  $Q_{j}$ ,
the principle automorphism is inner and is given by
(6.1)
$\Gamma(A)=WAW=W^{*}AW=WAW^{*}\qquad{\rm for\ all\ }A\in\mathfrak{C}^{n}\ .$
Let  $\{0,1\}^{n}$  be the set of fermion multi-indices, and for all  ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=(\alpha_{j})_{j}\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ ,
define  $Q^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=Q_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots Q_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}$  and  $|{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}|=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{j}$ .
Let  $\tau$  be the canonical trace on  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$ ,
determined by  $\tau(Q^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\delta_{0,|{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}|}$ .
In a standard representation of  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  as an algebra of operators on  $({\mathbb{C}}^{2})^{\otimes n}$  due to Brauer and Weyl,  $\tau$  is simply the normalized trace. See [11, 12] for references and further background.
Gross [33] defined a differential structure and a Dirichlet form on  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  as follows:
For  $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ , let  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  be given by
(6.2)
