${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Q_{j}A-\Gamma(A)Q_{j})\ .$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
Each  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  is a skew derivation. That is, for all  $A,B\in\mathfrak{C}^{n}$ ,
${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}(AB)=({{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}A)B+\Gamma(A){{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}B$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$ .
Gross defined the Dirichlet form  $\mathcal{E}(A,B)$  on  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  by
$\mathcal{E}(A,B)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tau[({{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}A)^{*}{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}B]$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$ , and defined the operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  on  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  by
$-\tau[A^{*}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}B]=\mathcal{E}(A,B)$ .
Simple computations show that for all  $A\in\mathfrak{C}^{n}$ ,
(6.3)
${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}^{\dagger}A=\frac{1}{2}\big(Q_{j}A+\Gamma(A)Q_{j}\big)\quad{\rm and}\quad{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\big(Q_{j}\Gamma(A)Q_{j}-A\big)\;.$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
It is evident that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}Q^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=-|{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}|Q^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}$ , hence  $-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is the fermion number operator.
When  $n$  is even, so that  $\Gamma(A)=W^{*}AW$ , we define  $V_{j}=iWQ_{j}$ , so that each
$V_{j}$  is both self-adjoint and unitary. Then, using the fact that  $V_{j}^{2}={{\bf 1}}$ , we may rewrite
(6.3) as
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\big(V_{j}AV_{j}-A\big)=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{n}[V_{j},[V_{j},A]]\ ,$
which has the form (3.6).
Thus,  $e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  is a QMS satisfying the  $\tau$ -DBC. Gross discussed this QMS as a fermionic analog of the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup; we refer to it as the infinite temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.
One good reason is that it is generated by the negative of the fermionic number operator.
Another is that as conjectured by Gross [33] and proved in [11], it has the same optimal hypercontractivity properties as the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. We shall further develop the analogy here.
(The infinite temperature part of the name will be justified in the next example.)
To relate the differential structure in (6.2) to the one considered here, note that when  $n$  is even, so that  $\Gamma$  is the inner automorphism given by (6.1), we have, with  $V_{j}$  defined as above,
(6.4)
${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}A=\frac{1}{2i}W[V_{j},A]=\frac{1}{2i}W\partial_{j}A\quad{\rm and}\quad{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}^{\dagger}A=-\frac{1}{2i}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}(WA)=-\frac{1}{2i}\partial_{j}(WA)$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
for  $j=1,\dots,n$ .
Thus, Gross’s differential structure in terms of skew derivations may be substituted with
the present differential structure in terms of derivations when  $n$  is even. When  $n$  is odd, this is
achieved by embedding  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  is an a larger Clifford algebra: One can add one more generator, or, perhaps better, embed the Clifford algebra generated by  $\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{n}\}$ , in the
phase space Clifford algebra with  $2n$  generators
$\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{n},P_{1},\dots,P_{n}\}$  that is discussed next.
6.2. The finite-temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be the Clifford algebra  $\mathfrak{C}^{n}$  of dimension  $n=2m$  for some  $m\in{\mathord{\mathbb{N}}}$ . Consider a set of generators
$\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\}\ ,$
where
$Q_{j}Q_{k}+Q_{k}Q_{j}=P_{j}P_{k}+P_{k}P_{j}=2\delta_{j,k}{{\bf 1}}\quad{\rm and}\quad Q_{j}P_{k}+P_{k}Q_{j}=0\quad{\rm for\ all}\ 1\leq j,k\leq m\ .$
We think of  $\mathcal{A}$  as the full set of phase space observables, the subalgebra generated by  $\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m}\}$  as the algebra of configuration space observables, and the subalgebra generated by  $\{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\}$  as the algebra of momentum space observables.
Form the operators
$Z_{j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(Q_{j}+iP_{j})\quad{\rm so\ that}\quad Z_{j}^{*}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(Q_{j}-iP_{j})\ .$
It is easy to check that
(6.5)
$Z_{j}Z_{k}+Z_{k}Z_{j}=0\quad\text{and}\quad Z_{j}Z_{k}^{*}+Z_{k}^{*}Z_{j}=2\delta_{j,k}{{\bf 1}}\quad{\rm for\ all}\ 1\leq j,k\leq m\ \ .$
Consider the complementary orthogonal projections  $N_{j}$  and  $N_{j}^{\perp}$  defined by
$N_{j}=\frac{1}{2}Z_{j}^{*}Z_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad N_{j}^{\perp}=\frac{1}{2}Z_{j}Z^{*}_{j}\quad{\rm for\ all}\ \ 1\leq j\leq m\ \ .$
Then (6.5) implies that
(6.6)
$Z_{j}N_{j}=N_{j}^{\perp}Z_{j}=Z_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad N_{j}Z_{j}=Z_{j}N_{j}^{\perp}=0\ .$
Note also that
(6.7)
$\displaystyle Z_{j}N_{k}=N_{k}Z_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad Z_{j}N_{k}^{\perp}=N_{k}^{\perp}Z_{j}\quad{\rm for\ all}\ \ j\neq k\ .$
Moreover,  $\{N_{1},\dots,N_{m},N_{1}^{\perp},\dots,N_{m}^{\perp}\}$  is a set of commuting orthogonal projections.
For each  $j$ ,  $Q_{j}P_{j}$  commutes with both  $Q_{k}$  and  $P_{k}$  for all  $k\neq j$ . Hence the operators
$\{Q_{1}P_{1},\dots,Q_{m}P_{m}\}$  all commute with one another. As in the previous example, let  $W=i^{m}\prod_{j=1}^{m}Q_{j}P_{j}$  so that  $W$  is self-adjoint and unitary, and for all  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ , let  $\Gamma(A)=WAW$ .
Note that  $Q_{j}P_{j}Z_{j}=iZ_{j}$  for each  $j$ .
For any set of  $m$  real numbers  $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}$ , and any parameter
$\beta\in(0,\infty)$ , to be interpreted as the inverse temperature, define the free Hamiltonian  $h$  and the Gibbs state  $\sigma_{\beta}$  by
$h=\sum_{j=1}^{m}e_{j}N_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad\sigma_{\beta}=\frac{1}{\tau[e^{-\beta h}]}e^{-\beta h}\ .$
where  $\tau$  is the canonical trace as in Section 6.1.
Since the  $N_{j}$  are commuting orthogonal projections,  $e^{-\beta h}$  is the product, in any order, of the operators  $e^{-\beta e_{j}}N_{j}+N_{j}^{\perp}$ .
Therefore, for each  $1\leq j\leq m$ ,
$\displaystyle\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}(Z_{j})=(e^{-\beta e_{j}}N_{j}+N_{j}^{\perp})Z_{j}(e^{\beta e_{j}}N_{j}+N_{j}^{\perp})=e^{\beta e_{j}}Z_{j}\ ,$
where we have used (6.6) and (6.7). Consequently,  $\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}(Z_{j}^{*})=e^{-\beta e_{j}}Z_{j}^{*}$ .
Since  $W$  commutes with every even element of  $\mathcal{A}$ , it follows that
$\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}(WZ_{j})=e^{\beta e_{j}}WZ_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}(Z_{j}^{*}W)=e^{-\beta e_{j}}Z_{j}^{*}W\ .$
Define the operators
$V_{j}=WZ_{j},\qquad 1\leq j\leq m\ ,$
so that  $\frac{1}{2}V_{j}^{*}V_{j}=N_{j}$  and  $\frac{1}{2}V_{j}V_{j}^{*}=N_{j}^{\perp}$ .
Then  $\{V_{1},\dots,V_{m},V_{1}^{*},\dots,V_{m}^{*}\}$  is set of operators on  $\mathcal{A}$  satisfying the conditions (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) of Theorem 3.1.
Therefore, the operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$  defined by
(6.8)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}A=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left[e^{\beta e_{j}/2}\Big(V_{j}^{*}[A,V_{j}]+[V_{j}^{*},A]V_{j}\Big)+e^{-\beta e_{j}/2}\Big(V_{j}[A,V_{j}^{*}]+[V_{j},A]V_{j}^{*}\Big)\right]$
is the generator of a QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}}$  that satisfies the  $\sigma_{\beta}$ -DBC.
It is a simple matter to diagonalize  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$ :
For each  $1\leq j\leq m$ , define the four operators
$K_{j,(0,0)}={{\bf 1}}\ ,\quad K_{j,(1,0)}=Z_{j}\ ,\quad K_{j,(0,1)}=Z^{*}_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad K_{j,(1,1)}=e^{\beta e_{j}/2}N_{j}-e^{-\beta e_{j}/2}N_{j}^{\perp}\ .$
One readily checks that this set of four operators is orthonormal in any of the inner products  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  based on  $\sigma_{\beta}$ .
Using the fact that for each  $j$ ,  $V_{j}$  and  $V_{j}^{*}$  commute with  $P_{k}$  and  $Q_{k}$  for all  $k\neq j$ , and using the identities  $V_{j}K_{j,(1,1)}=e^{\beta e_{j}/2}V_{j}$  and  $K_{j,(1,1)}V_{j}=-e^{-\beta e_{j}/2}V_{j}$  , we readily compute that
(6.9)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}Z_{j}=-\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)Z_{j}\quad{\rm and}\quad{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}K_{j,(1,1)}=-2\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)K_{j,(1,1)}\ .$
Therefore, for all  $0\leq k,\ell\leq 1$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}K_{j,(k,\ell)}=-(k+\ell)\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)K_{j,(k,\ell)}\ .$
Let  ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m})$  denote a generic element of the index set  $\{\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}\}^{m}$ ,
and for  $\alpha=(k,\ell)\in\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}$ , define  $|\alpha|=k+\ell$ . Then the functions
$K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:=K_{1,\alpha_{1}}K_{2,\alpha_{2}}\cdots K_{m,\alpha_{m}}$
are an orthogonal (but not normalized) basis for  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  consisting of eigenvectors of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$ :
(6.10)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=-\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}|\alpha_{j}|\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)\right)K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\ .$
It is now easy to check that in the infinite temperature limit (i.e.,  $\beta\to 0$ ),
$\lim_{\beta\to 0}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  where
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left([V_{j},[V_{j}^{*},A]]+[V_{j}^{*},[V_{j},A]]\right)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(Q_{j}\Gamma(A)Q_{j}+P_{j}\Gamma(A)P_{j}^{*}-2A\right)\ ,$
From the previous example, we recognize  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}$  as the negative of the number operator on  $\mathcal{A}=\mathfrak{C}^{n}$ . That is,
in the infinite temperature limit ( $\beta\to 0$ ), we recover the infinite temperature
Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, justifying our nomenclature.
As in the infinite temperature case, there is a differential calculus that is more closely adapted to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$ :
For  $1\leq j\leq m$ , define the operators
${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}A=\frac{1}{2}(Z_{j}A-\Gamma(A)Z_{j})=\frac{1}{2}W[V_{j},A]\quad{\rm and}\quad\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}A=\frac{1}{2}(Z_{j}^{*}A-\Gamma(A)Z_{j}^{*})=-\frac{1}{2}W[V_{j}^{*},A]$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
We readily compute that
(6.11)
$\displaystyle{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,(0,0)}={{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,(1,0)}=0\ ,\quad{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,(0,1)}$
$\displaystyle=K_{j,(0,0)}$
$\displaystyle\quad{\rm and}\quad{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,1,1}$
$\displaystyle=\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)K_{j,(1,0)}\ ,$
and that
(6.12)
$\displaystyle\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,(0,0)}=\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower ,\quad\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,(1,0)}$
$\displaystyle=K_{j,(0,0)}$
$\displaystyle\quad{\rm and}\quad\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}K_{j,(1,1)}$
$\displaystyle=-\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)K_{j,(0,1)}\ .$
Again using the fact that for each  $j$ ,  $V_{j}$  and  $V_{j}^{*}$  commute with
$P_{k}$  and  $Q_{k}$  for all  $k\neq j$ , one determines the effect of  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  and  $\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  on all of  $\mathcal{A}$ .
The orthonormal basis  $\{K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\}$  may be viewed as consisting of analogs of multivariate Krawtchouck polynomials – the discrete analogs of the Hermite polynomials.
The differential operators  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  and  $\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$ , which are skew derivations as in the infinite temperature case, have the advantage over the closely related derivations  $\partial_{j}A=[V_{j},A]$  and  $\overline{\partial}_{j}A=[V_{j}^{*},A]$  that they always lower the “degree” of any  $K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}$  by one,
as one would expect.
The operators
$\partial_{j}A$  and  $\overline{\partial}_{j}A$  do not do this.
Using (6.11) and (6.12) one readily deduces the identities, valid for all
(6.13)
${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule $\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
and
(6.14)
$\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=-\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\ .$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$
Finally, we observe that each of the vectors  $K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}$  is an eigenvector of  $\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}$ . Moreover, it is easy to see that if  $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}$  is linearly independent over the integers,
then  $\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}$  if and only if for each  $k$ ,  $|\alpha_{k}|\neq 1$ .
The span of the set of such  $K_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}$  is the same as the span of
(6.15)
$\{N_{1},N_{1}^{\perp},\dots,N_{m},N_{m}^{\perp}\}\ .$
Hence in this case, the modular algebra  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma_{\beta}}$  is the algebra generated by the commuting projections in (6.15).
Let us denote this algebra, which does not depend on  $\beta$ , by  $\mathcal{B}$ .
While it need not be the modular algebra when  $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}$  is not linearly independent over the integers, it is easy to see (by continuity or computation) that it is always invariant under  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ .
The projections in (6.15) are not minimal in  $\mathcal{B}$ , but the set of the  $2^{m}$  distinct non-zero products one can form from them is a full set of minimal projections.
We may identify this set with the discrete hypercube  ${\mathord{\mathscr{Q}}}^{m}=\{0,1\}^{m}$ .
Set  ${\mathcal{J}}=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ , and let  $s_{j}:{\mathord{\mathscr{Q}}}^{m}\to{\mathord{\mathscr{Q}}}^{m}$  define the  $j$ -th coordinate swap defined by  $s_{j}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})=(x_{1},\ldots,-x_{j},\ldots,x_{m})$ .
Let  ${\boldsymbol{x}}$  denote a generic point of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{Q}}}^{m}$ .
Define  ${\displaystyle E_{\boldsymbol{x}}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}N_{j}^{x_{1}}(N_{j}^{\perp})^{1-x_{1}}}$ .
The restriction  ${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.37502pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.94775pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.94775pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.3988pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=4.50006pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}}_{t}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$  of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  to  $\mathcal{B}$  is a nearest neighbor random walk on  ${\mathord{\mathscr{Q}}}^{m}$  with transition rates that are readily computed using Theorem 4.2.
For a standard representation in which the elements of  $\mathcal{A}$  operate on  ${\mathbb{C}}^{2^{m}}$ , and  $\tau$  is the normalized trace, each  $E_{\boldsymbol{x}}$  is rank one, so that the transition rate matrix  $D$  defined in (4.2) is simply  $D_{{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}}={\rm Tr}[E_{\boldsymbol{x}},{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}E_{{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}}]$ .
Using (6.9) through (6.10), one readily computes that  $D_{{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}}=0$  unless  ${\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}=s_{j}({\boldsymbol{x}})$  for some  $j$ , and in that case
$D_{{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}{\displaystyle\frac{2\cosh(\beta e_{j})}{1+e^{-\beta e_{j}}}}&x_{j}=1\\
{\displaystyle\frac{2\cosh(\beta e_{j})}{1+e^{\beta e_{j}}}}&x_{j}=0\ ,\end{cases}$
and this gives the jump rates along the edges of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{Q}}}^{m}$  for the classical Markov chain corresponding to  ${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.37502pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.94775pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.94775pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.3988pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=4.50006pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}}_{t}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$ .
6.3. The Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup
A set  $\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\}$  of self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space  $\mathcal{H}$  is a representation of the Canonical Commutation Relations (CCR), in case for all  $1\leq j,k\leq m$ ,
$[Q_{j},Q_{k}]=0\ ,\quad[P_{j},P_{k}]=0\quad{\rm and}\quad[Q_{j},P_{k}]=i\delta_{j,k}{{\bf 1}}\ .$
All representations of the CCR are necessarily infinite-dimensional, since otherwise we would have  ${\rm Tr}[[Q_{j},P_{j}]]=0$  which is incompatible with  $[Q_{j},P_{j}]=i{{\bf 1}}$ . The CCR algebra is the  $C^{*}$ -algebra generated by the unitaries
$\{e^{-t_{1}Q_{1}},\dots,e^{it_{m}Q_{m}},e^{-s_{1}P_{1}},\dots,e^{is_{m}P_{m}}\}$  for all  $t_{1},\dots,t_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{m}$ , or, what is the essentially the same thing, the Weyl operators.
Not only is  $\mathcal{H}$  necessarily infinite-dimensional, but the operators  $\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\}$  are unbounded.
Therefore, the CCR algebra for  $m$  Bose degrees of freedom lies outside the scope of the theory being developed in this paper.
However, even without fully extending this theory to infinite dimensions, we shall be able to deduce new results for an important QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$ , namely the Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.
To keep things simple in this excursion into the infinite-dimensional case, we take  $m=1$ .
Exactly as in the Fermi case, we form the operators
$Z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(Q+iP)\quad{\rm so\ that}\quad Z^{*}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(Q-iP)\ .$
It is easy to check that
(6.16)
$[Z,Z^{*}]={{\bf 1}}\ .$
In one standard representation that we may as well fix here,  $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}({\mathbb{R}},\gamma(x){\rm d}x)$  where  $\gamma(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2}$  and  $Z=\partial/\partial x$ .
Then a simple computation shows that  $Z^{*}=x-\partial/\partial x$ , and (6.16) is satisfied.
Define the Hamiltonian  $h$  by  $h=Z^{*}Z$ .
It is evident that for each  $k$ , the linear space of polynomials in  $x$  of degree at most  $k$  is invariant under  $h$ .
Since  $h$  is self-adjoint, this means the eigenfunctions of  $h$  are orthogonal polynomials in  $\mathcal{H}$ , and hence are the Hermite polynomials.
It is well known and easy to check that the  $k$ th Hermite polynomial is an eigenfunction of  $h$  with eigenvalue  $k$ .
That is,  $h$  is the Bose number operator (for one degree of freedom).
Fixing an inverse temperature  $\beta\in(0,\infty)$ , we define  $\sigma_{\beta}$  as
$\sigma_{\beta}=\Big({\rm Tr}\big[e^{-\beta h}\big]\Big)^{-1}e^{-\beta h}\ .$
Note that  ${\rm Tr}\left[e^{-\beta h}\right]$  is finite by what we have said concerning the spectrum of  $h$ .
One readily finds that
$[Z,h]=Z$ ,
which is the differential version of the identity
$\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}(Z)=e^{\beta}Z\ .$
It follows that  $Z$  and  $Z^{*}$  are eigenfunctions of the modular operator.
(Note that since they are unbounded, they do not belong to the CCR algebra, and are only affiliated to its von Neumann algebra closure.)
Define  $V_{1}=Z$  and  $V_{2}=Z^{*}$ . Then  $\{V_{1},V_{2}\}$  is a set of operators satisfying conditions (iii) and (iv) of Theorem 3.1 (with  $\omega_{1}=-\beta$  and  $\omega_{2}=\beta$ ), but not conditions (i) and (ii), since in the infinite-dimensional case, it is in general too much to ask that the  $V_{j}$  be trace-class. (However, since  $V_{1}$ ,  $V_{2}$  and  ${{\bf 1}}$  are eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  with distinct eigenvalues there is a natural sense in which they are orthogonal so that a natural analog of (i) and (ii) is valid.)
In any case, we may define
(6.17)
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}A$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left[e^{\beta/2}\Big(Z^{*}[A,Z]+[Z^{*},A]Z\Big)+e^{-\beta/2}\Big(Z[A,Z^{*}]+[Z,A]Z^{*}\Big)\right]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle e^{\beta/2}\left(Z^{*}AZ-\tfrac{1}{2}\{Z^{*}Z,A\}\right)+e^{-\beta/2}\left(ZAZ^{*}-\tfrac{1}{2}\{ZZ^{*},A\}\right)\ ,$
where  $\{A,B\}$  denotes the anti-commutator  $AB+BA$ .
The operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$  is in fact the generator of an ergodic QMS, as shown in [18].
These authors construct the QMS first on the infinite-dimensional analog of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ , which in this case strictly contains  $\mathcal{A}$ , and then show that the resulting semigroup has the Feller property; i.e., it preserves  $\mathcal{A}$ .
In [18], another detailed balance condition based on self-adjointness with respect to the KMS inner product is used.
However, Theorem 2.9 and what we have said above about the modular operator shows that the semigroup also satisfies the  $\sigma_{\beta}$ -DBC as defined here.
In this sense, the example falls into our framework.
Simple computations show that for  $\partial_{1}A=[Z,A]$  and  $\partial_{2}A=[Z^{*},A]$ ,
(6.18)
$\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}A-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}\partial_{j}A=-\sinh(\beta/2)\partial_{j}A$
for  $j=1,2$  and all  $A$  in a dense
domain of analytic vectors for  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$  that is discussed in [18].
We shall use this identity on this domain later to prove a sharp entropy dissipation inequality for this semigroup, as conjectured in [38, equation (9)]. Note that the corresponding formula for the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup involves  $\cosh$  in place of  $\sinh$ . This reflects the fact that in the Fermi case, taking the infinite temperature limit ( $\beta\to 0$ ) yields a
QMS with a stationary state, while for the Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, this is not the case: the  $\beta\to 0$  limit cannot be taken in (6.3).
The modular generator  $h$  has non-degenerate spectrum, and so the modular algebra
$\mathcal{A}_{\sigma_{\beta}}$  in this case is simply the set of all operators that commute with
$\sigma_{\beta}$ , which is the same thing as the algebra generated by the
spectral projections of  $h$ . In particular,
$\mathcal{A}_{\sigma_{\beta}}$  is commutative and independent of  $\beta$ .
It is easy to see that the restriction
${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.37502pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.94775pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.94775pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.3988pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=4.50006pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$}\crcr}}}}}_{t}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.80557pt}$  of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  to  $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma_{\beta}}$  corresponds, as in
Theorem 4.2, to a birth-death process on  ${\mathord{\mathbb{N}}}$ .
7. Riemannian metrics and gradient flow
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the
$\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ .
In this section we define a Riemannian metric on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  that is determined by  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ , and for which, as we shall see, the flow given by the dual semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$ , is gradient flow for the relative entropy with respect to  $\sigma$ .
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be given in the standard form (3.4).
Throughout this section,  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  are fixed, and we assume that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is ergodic.
Let  $\rho(t),t\in(t_{0},t_{1})$ , be any differentiable path in  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  regarded as a convex subset of  $\mathcal{A}$ .
For each  $t\in(t_{0},t_{1})$ , let  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(t)\in\mathcal{A}$  denote the derivative of  $\rho(t)$  in  $t$ .
If  $\rho(t)$  is any differentiable path in  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  defined on  $(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$  for some  $\epsilon>0$  such that  $\rho(0)=\rho_{0}$ , then  ${\rm Tr}[\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)]=0$ , so that by Theorem 5.4, there is an affine subspace of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  consisting of elements  ${\bf A}$  for which
(7.1)
$\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=\dive{\bf A}\ .$
We wish to rewrite (7.1) as an analog of the classical continuity equation for the time evolution of a probability density  $\rho(x,t)$  on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ :
(7.2)
$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho(x,t)+\dive[{\bf v}(x,t)\rho(x,t)]=0\ .$
In the classical case, for  $\rho$  strictly positive, any expression of the form
(7.3)
$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho(x,t)=\dive[{\bf a}(x,t)]$
gives rise to (7.2) with  ${\bf v}(x,t)=-\rho^{-1}(x,t){\bf a}(x,t)$ .
Conversely, given (7.2) and defining
${\bf a}(x,t)=-\rho(x,t){\bf v}(x,t)$ , (7.3) is satisfied.
In the quantum case, there are many different ways to multiply and divide by  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ .
Definition 5.7 gives a one-parameter family of ways to multiply  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  by  $\rho$  that is relevant here.
In the next definition, we extend this to multiplication of vector fields  ${\bf A}\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  by  $\rho$ .
7.1 DEFINITION.
Let  $\vec{\omega}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}$ . For  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  we define the linear operator  $[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}$  on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  by
$[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\big(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)=\big([\rho]_{\omega_{1}}A_{1},\dots,[\rho]_{\omega_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)\ .$
Note that  $[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}$  is invertible with
(7.4)
$[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}^{-1}\big(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)=\big([\rho]_{\omega_{1}}^{-1}A_{1},\dots,[\rho]_{\omega_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}}^{-1}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)\ .$
where we have used the fact that  $R_{\rho}$  and  $\Delta_{\rho}$  commute.
We are now ready to write (7.1) in the form of a continuity equation:
Pick some  $\vec{\omega}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}$ , and define  ${\bf V}$  by  ${\bf V}=-[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}^{-1}{\bf A}$ .
Then evidently (7.1) becomes
(7.5)
$\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)+\dive([\rho]_{{\vec{\omega}}}{\bf V})=0\ .$
The vector field  ${\bf A}$  in (7.1) is not unique; however according to Theorem 5.4, the set of such vector fields is an affine space, and thus, in our finite-dimensional setting a closed convex set.
It follows immediately that while the vector field  ${\bf V}$  in (7.5) is not unique,
the set of such vector fields is a closed affine subspace of  $\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}$ , and consequently there is a unique element of minimal norm in
$\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}$  for any Hilbertian norm on  $\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}$ . We now define the class of Hilbertian norms that is relevant here:
7.2 DEFINITION.
For each  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and the given generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ ,
define an inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}}$
on  $\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}$  by
$\langle{\bf W},{\bf V}\rangle_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\bf W}_{j},[\rho]_{\omega_{j}}{\bf V}_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .$
We write  $\|{\bf V}\|_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}}$  for the corresponding Hilbertian norm.
This norm can be viewed as a non-commutative analog of a weighted  $L^{2}$ -norm for vector fields.
7.3 THEOREM.
Let  $\rho(t)$  be a differentiable path in  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  defined on
$(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$  for some  $\epsilon>0$  such that  $\rho(0)=\rho_{0}$ .
Then there is a unique vector field  ${\bf V}\in\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}$  of the form  ${\bf V}=\nabla U$  with  $U\in{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}$ , for which the non-commutative continuity equation
(7.6)
$\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}{\bf V})=-\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla U)$
holds. Moreover,  $U$  can be taken to be traceless, and is then self-adjoint and uniquely determined. Furthermore, if  ${\bf W}$  is any other vector field such that  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}{\bf W})$ , then
$\|{\bf V}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}<\|{\bf W}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}\ .$
Proof.
In view of the discussion above, it remains to show that the unique norm-minimizing vector field  ${\bf V}$  is a gradient. To see this, let  ${\bf A}$  be an arbitrary divergence-free vector field, set  ${\bf W}:=[\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}^{-1}{\bf A}$ , and  ${\bf V}_{\varepsilon}:={\bf V}+\varepsilon{\bf W}$ , so that  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)+\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}{\bf V}_{\varepsilon})=0$  for all  $\varepsilon$ . Since  $\|{\bf V}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}<\|{\bf V}_{\varepsilon}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}$  for all  $\varepsilon$ , it follows that  $\langle{\bf V},{\bf W}\rangle_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}}=0$ , and therefore  $\langle{{\bf V},{\bf A}}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=0$ . This means that  ${\bf V}$  is orthogonal to the set of divergence-free vector fields, hence it is the gradient of some  $U\in{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}$ . By subtracting a multiple of the identity, we may take  $U$  to be traceless, and then  $U$  is uniquely determined, in view of Theorem 5.3 and the ergodicity of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ .
To show that  $U$  is self adjoint, define the operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}$  by
(7.7)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A=\dive([\rho_{\vec{\omega}}]\nabla A)\ .$
A direct computation yields
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\left([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}(V_{j}A-AV_{j})\right)V_{j}^{*}-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}V_{j}^{*}\left([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}(V_{j}A-AV_{j})\right)\ .$
Then using (5.10) of Lemma 5.8,
$({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A)^{*}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\left([\rho]_{-\omega_{j}}(V_{j}^{*}A^{*}-A^{*}V_{j}^{*})\right)V_{j}-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}V_{j}\left([\rho]_{-\omega_{j}}(V_{j}^{*}A^{*}-A^{*}V_{j}^{*})\right)\ .$
Now use the fact that  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}=\{V_{j}^{*}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  and that for all  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ ,  $\Delta_{\sigma}(V_{j})=e^{-\omega_{j}}V_{j}$  and  $\Delta_{\sigma}(V_{j}^{*})=e^{\omega_{j}}V_{j}^{*}$ . It follows that
$({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A^{*}$ .
Using (7.7) we write (7.6) as  ${\displaystyle\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho(0)}U}$  for the  $U$  found above. Since  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)$  is self-adjoint, it follows from what we have just shown that we also have  ${\displaystyle\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho(0)}U^{*}}$ . By the uniqueness of  $U$ ,  $U$  is self-adjoint.
∎
7.4 DEFINITION.
For each  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , we identify the tangent space  $T_{\rho}$  at  $\rho=\rho_{0}$ , with the set of gradients vector fields  $\mathcal{G}:=\{\nabla U\ :\ U\in{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}\ ,\ U=U^{*}\}$  through the one-to-one correspondence provided by (7.6).
We define the Riemannian metric  $g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  by
$\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)\|^{2}_{g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}}=\|{\bf V}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}^{2}\ $
where  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)$  and  ${\bf V}$  are related by (7.6).
The metric we have just defined is  $C^{\infty}$ . Indeed, let  $\mathcal{A}$  be  $m$ -dimensional and let
${A_{1},\dots,A_{m-1}}$  be an orthonormal set of  $m-1$  self-adjoint traceless elements of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ .
Then we can define a coordinate map  $u:{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{m-1}$  by
$u(\rho)=\big({\rm Tr}[A_{1}\rho],\dots,{\rm Tr}[A_{m-1}\rho]\big)\ .$
Note that  $u(\tau)=0$ . Evidently  $u$  is a one-to-one map of  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  onto an open bounded convex subset of  ${\mathbb{R}}^{m-1}$ . We give  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , as usual, the corresponding differential structure. Conveniently, an atlas of just one chart covers the manifold.
Let  $u^{k}(\rho)={\rm Tr}[A_{k}\rho]$  by the  $k$ th coordinate function. The  $k$ th coordinate vector field is tangent
to the curve  $t\mapsto\rho+tA_{k}$  for  $t$  in the open interval in which the right hand side belongs to
${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ . The operator  $\dive[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla$  is invertible on
the orthogonal complement of the identity; i.e., on the span of  ${A_{1},\dots,A_{m-1}}$ . Define the
$k$ th potential function  $X_{k}(\rho)$  to be the unique traceless solution  $X$  of
$\dive[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla X=A_{k}\ .$
It then follows that for the curve  $t\mapsto\rho+tA_{k}$ ,  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=\dive[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla X_{k}(\rho)$ . This means that the  $k$ th coordinate tangent vector field
$\partial/\partial u^{k}$  is given by
$\frac{\partial}{\partial u^{k}}=\nabla X_{k}(\rho)\ ,$
Therefore, in this coordinate system, the  $k,\ell$  component of the metric tensor is given by
$[g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(\rho)]_{k,\ell}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle\nabla X_{k}(\rho),[\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\nabla X_{\ell}(\rho)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ ,$
By Lemma 5.8, for each  $j$ ,  $\rho\mapsto[\rho]_{\omega_{j}}$  is  $C^{\infty}$ , and it follows from this that the map  $\rho\mapsto[\dive[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla]^{-1}$ , where the inverse is the inverse on the orthogonal complement of  ${{\bf 1}}$ , is  $C^{\infty}$ . Thus, for each  $k,\ell$ ,
$[g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(\rho)]_{k,\ell}$  is a  $C^{\infty}$  function of  $\rho$ .
Now let  ${\mathcal{F}}:{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}\to{\mathbb{R}}$  be a differentiable function.
The differential of  ${\mathcal{F}}$ , denoted  ${\displaystyle\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho)}$ , is the unique traceless self-adjoint element in  $\mathcal{A}$  satisfying
(7.8)
$\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}\big({\mathcal{F}}(\rho+tA)-{\mathcal{F}}(\rho)\big)={\rm Tr}\left[\displaystyle\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho)A\right]$
for all traceless self-adjoint  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .
This notation is traditional in the context of gradient flows for the  $2$ -Wasserstein metric, and it
allows us to reserve the symbol  $D$  for covariant derivatives on our Riemannian manifold.)
The corresponding gradient vector field, denoted  ${\rm grad}_{g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}}{\mathcal{F}}(\rho)$ , will be interpreted using the identification of the tangent space given in Definition 7.4: it is the unique element in  $\mathcal{G}$  satisfying
(7.9)
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathcal{F}}(\rho(t))\bigg|_{t=0}=\big\langle{\mathrm{grad}_{g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}}{\mathcal{F}}(\rho),\nabla U}\big\rangle_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}$
for all differentiable paths  $\rho(t)$  defined on  $(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$  for some  $\epsilon>0$  with  $\rho(0)=\rho$  and  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)+\dive([\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla U)=0$  for some self-adjoint  $U$ .
Combining (7.8) and (7.9), it follows that
$\displaystyle-\Big\langle{\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho),\,\dive\big([\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla U\big)}\Big\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=\big\langle{\mathrm{grad}_{g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}}{\mathcal{F}}(\rho),\,[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla U}\big\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}}\ .$
Since this argument holds for arbitrary paths  $\rho(t)$ , Theorem 7.3 implies that this identity holds for arbitrary  $U$ . Therefore, we have proved:
7.5 THEOREM.
For a differentiable function  ${\mathcal{F}}$  on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ ,
the Riemannian gradient of  ${\mathcal{F}}$  with respect to the Riemannian metric  $g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  is given by
${\rm grad}_{g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}}{\mathcal{F}}(\rho)=\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho)\ ,$
and the corresponding gradient flow equation (for steepest descent) is
$\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(t)=\dive\Big([\rho(t)]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho(t))\Big)\ .$
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be a QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the
$\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ .
Recall that the relative entropy with respect to  $\sigma$  is the functional  $D(\cdot\|\sigma)$  on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  defined by (1.1).
An easy calculation shows that for  ${\mathcal{F}}(\rho)=D(\rho||\sigma)$ ,
$\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}=\log\rho-\log\sigma\ .$
Therefore, Theorem 5.10 and Theorem 7.5 yield:
7.6 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be QMS on  $\mathcal{A}$  that satisfies the
$\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ . Then
(7.10)
$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho$
is gradient flow for the relative entropy  $D(\cdot||\sigma)$  in the metric
$g_{\rho,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  canonically associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  through its representation in the form (3.4).
In [12], we proved the special case of Theorem 7.6 in which  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is the infinite temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, except that there we defined the metric in terms of the differential calculus associated to the skew derivations  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$ , defined in (6.2) instead of the derivations  $\partial_{j}$  used here. The two metrics are in fact the same, and the alternate form of the metric in terms of the skew derivatives will be useful to us in the next section.
Therefore we explain the equivalence, using the notation introduced in section 6. Let  $\rho(t)$  be a smooth path in  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathfrak{C}^{n})$  defined on a neighborhood of  $0$  with  $\rho(0)=\rho$ .
Suppose that
(7.11)
$\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\partial_{j}([\rho]_{0}\partial_{j}U)$
for some self-adjoint  $U\in\mathfrak{C}^{n}$ . (We recall that since  $V_{j}$  is self-adjoint in this case,
$\partial_{j}^{\dagger}=\partial_{j}$ , and that  $\omega_{j}=0$  for each  $j$ .)
Then by (6.4) and the integral representation for  $[\rho]_{0}$ , we can rewrite (7.11) as
$\displaystyle\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-4\sum_{j=1}^{n}{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}(W[\rho]_{0}(W{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U))=-4\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{0}^{1}{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}(W\rho^{s}W{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U\rho^{1-s}){\rm d}s$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-4\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{0}^{1}{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}(\Gamma(\rho^{s}){{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U\rho^{1-s}){\rm d}s\ .$
The operation  $A\mapsto\int_{0}^{1}\Gamma(\rho^{s})A\rho^{1-s}{\rm d}s$  is precisely the non-commutative
analog of “multiplication by  $\rho$ ” that was used in [12]. Thus apart form the trivial factor of  $4$ ,
the realization of the tangent space and interpretation of continuity equation in [12] is the same as it is here;
the two formulation of the continuity equation are equivalent.
The same applies to the metric. With  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)$  as above,
$\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)\|_{g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}^{2}$  as we have defined it here is given by
$\displaystyle\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)\|_{g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\langle{\partial_{j},U[\rho]_{0}\partial_{j}U}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathfrak{C}^{n}}}=4\sum_{j=1}^{n}\langle W{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U,[\rho]_{0}(W{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathfrak{C}^{n}}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle 4\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{0}^{1}\langle{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U,\Gamma(\rho^{s}){{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}U\rho^{1-s}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathfrak{C}^{n}}}{\rm d}s\ .$
The ultimate term in (7) is, apart from a trivial factor of  $4$ , precisely
how the metric tensor was defined in [12].
This shows two things: First, that Theorem 7.6 is an extension, and not merely an analog, of our work in [12]. Second, it makes available to us the differential calculus based on the skew derivations when studying the geometry associated to the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. (We have explicitly discussed the infinite temperature case, but the same reasoning applies in general.) Since the skew derivations have the property of “lowering polynomial degree by one” for the eigenfunctions of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ , as discussed between (6.12) and (6.13), this alternate formulation of the metric will be extremely helpful in the next section.
8. Geodesic convexity and relaxation to equilibrium
In this section we develop the advantages of having written the evolution equation (7.10) as gradient flow for the relative entropy.
We draw on work of Otto and Westdickenberg [57] and Daneri and Savaré [20].
Both pairs of authors were primarily interested in infinite-dimensional problems concerning metrics on spaces of probability densities, but several of their results are new and interesting in finite dimension.
The approach of Otto and Westdickenberg is thoroughly developed in the finite-dimensional setting in Section 2 of [20].
We briefly summarize what we need.
Let  $(\mathcal{M},g)$  be any smooth, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
For  $x,y$  in  $\mathcal{M}$ , the Riemannian distance  $d_{g}(x,y)$  between  $x$  and  $y$  is given by minimizing an action integral of paths  $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M}$  running from  $x$  to  $y$ :
$d_{g}^{2}(x,y)=\inf\left\{\int_{0}^{1}\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s)\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(s))}\>{\rm d}s\ :\ \gamma(0)=x,\ \gamma(1)=y\right\}\ ,$
where
$\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s)\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(s))}=g_{\gamma(s)}(\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s),\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s))\ .$
(If the infimum is achieved, any minimizer  $\gamma$  will be a geodesic.)
If  $F$  is a smooth function on  $\mathcal{M}$ ,
let  ${\rm grad}_{g}F$  denote its Riemannian gradient. Consider the semigroup  $S_{t}$
of transformations on  $\mathcal{M}$
given by solving  $\dot{\gamma}(t)=-{\rm grad}_{g}F(\gamma(t))$ ; we assume for now that nice global solutions exist. The semigroup  $S_{t}$ ,  $t\geq 0$ , is gradient flow for  $F$ .
For  $\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , the function  $F$  is  $\lambda$ -convex in case whenever  $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M}$  is a distance minimizing geodesic, then for all  $s\in(0,1)$ ,
$\frac{{\rm d}^{2}}{{\rm d}s^{2}}F(\gamma(s))\geq\lambda g(\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s),\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s))\ .$
It is a standard result that whenever  $F$  is  $\lambda$ -convex, the gradient flow for  $F$  is  $\lambda$ -contracting in the sense that for all  $x,y\in\mathcal{M}$  and  $t>0$ ,
(8.1)
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq-2\lambda d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\ .$
Otto and Westdickenberg [57] developed an approach to geodesic convexity that takes (8.1) as its starting point.
Let  $\{\gamma(s)\}_{s\in[0,1]}$  be any smooth path in  $\mathcal{M}$  with  $\gamma(0)=x$  and  $\gamma(1)=y$ .
They use the gradient flow transformation  $S_{t}$  to define a one-parameter family of paths  $\gamma^{t}:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M}$ ,  $t\geq 0$  defined by
$\gamma^{t}(s)=S_{t}\gamma(s)\ .$
Since  $\gamma^{t}$  is admissible for the variational problem that defines  $d_{g}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))$ , it is immediate that for each  $t\geq 0$ ,
(8.2)
$d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq\int_{0}^{1}\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma^{t}(s))}\>{\rm d}s\ .$
In the present smooth setting it is shown in [20, (2.8) – (2.11)] that if for all smooth curves
$\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M}$ ,
(8.3)
