$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\bigg|_{0+}\left(\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma^{t}(s))}\right)\leq-2\lambda\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma^{0}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma^{0}(s))}\ ,$
for all  $s\in(0,1)$ , then  $F$  is geodesically  $\lambda$ -convex.
To see the connection between (8.3) and the contraction property, suppose that  $x$  and  $y$  are connected by a minimal geodesic  $\gamma$  so that
$d_{g}^{2}(x,y)=\int_{0}^{1}\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(s))}\>{\rm d}s\ .$
(If  $x$  and  $y$  are sufficiently close, this is the case.)
Then (8.2) and (8.3) combine to yield
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\bigg|_{0+}d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq-2\lambda d_{g}^{2}(x,y)\ ,$
and then, provided that  $S_{t}(x)$  and  $S_{t}(y)$  continue to be connected by a minimal geodesic for all  $t$ , the semigroup property of  $S_{t}$  yields the exponential  $\lambda$ -contractivity of the flow:
(8.4)
$d_{g}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq e^{-\lambda t}d_{g}(x,y)\ .$
The local argument in [20] proves the geodesic  $\lambda$ -convexity of  $F$  when (8.3) is valid for all smooth paths in  $\mathcal{M}$ , and thus leads to (8.4) without any assumptions of geodesic completeness.
When (8.3) is valid for some  $\lambda>0$ , and hence also (8.4) for the same  $\lambda$ ,  $F$  has at most one fixed point  $x_{0}$  in  $\mathcal{M}$ , which is necessarily a strict minimizer of  $F$  on  $\mathcal{M}$ .
We may normalize  $F(x_{0})=0$ , and then under the geodesic  $\lambda$ -convexity of  $F$ , is it well known that for all  $x$ ,
(8.5)
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}F(S_{t}(x))\leq-2\lambda F(S_{t}(x))\ ,$
which gives us another way to measure the rate of convergence to the fixed point under the flow  $S_{t}$ .
There is also a more direct route from (8.3) to (8.5).
If  $\gamma(t)$  is given by the gradient flow of  $F$  through  $\gamma(t)=S_{t}(x)$ , then
(8.6)
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}F(\gamma(t))=-\|{\rm grad}_{g}F(\gamma(t))\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(t))}\ .$
Define the energy function  $E$  associated to  $F$  by
(8.7)
$E(x)=\|{\rm grad}_{g}F(x)\|^{2}_{g(x)}\ .$
Then (8.3) applied with  $\gamma^{t}(s)=S_{s+t}(x)$
together with the semigroup property yields
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}E(S_{t}(x))\leq-2\lambda E(S_{t}(x))\ .$
Hence (8.3) not only leads to the contractivity property (8.4), but also to the exponential convergence estimates
(8.8)
$F(S_{t}(x))\leq e^{-2\lambda t}F(x)\quad{\rm and}\quad E(S_{t}(x))\leq e^{-2\lambda t}E(x)\ .$
Moreover, combining (8.8) with (8.6) and (8.7), we obtain the inequality
(8.9)
$F(x)\leq\frac{1}{2\lambda}E(x)\ .$
In our setting, when  $F$  is a relative entropy function, (8.9) will be a
generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality.
The relations between (8.4) and the bounds in (8.8) and geodesic convexity of  $F$  have all been discussed by Otto [55] as the basis of his approach to quantitative estimates on the rates of relaxation for solutions of the porous medium equation.
Thus, to prove geodesic convexity of  $F$ , and hence (8.4) and (8.8), it suffices to prove (8.3).
This first derivative estimate can provide a much easier route to a proof of  $\lambda$ -convexity of  $F$  than direct calculation of the Hessian of  $F$  followed by an estimate of its least eigenvalue.
The point of view of Otto and Westdickenberg is that this approach can be especially fruitful in an infinite-dimensional setting (such as that of [55]) given all the regularity issues to go along with computing the Hessian of  $F$ .
In the remainder of this section, we shall show that it is also quite fruitful in our finite-dimensional setting.
Related work in the commutative setting can be found in [23, 24, 28, 45, 47, 49].
For the difficulties relating to direct computation and analysis of the Hessian even for the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, see our previous paper [12].
8.1. Geodesic convexity using intertwining relations
For the rest of this section, let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and fix  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ , an ergodic QMS that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be given in the standard form (3.4), so that the data specifying
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  are the sets  $\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}$ .
Let  $\nabla:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  and  $\dive:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  be the associated non-commutative gradient and divergence (as opposed to the associated Riemannian gradient and divergence).
Let  $\rho:[0,1]\to{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  be a smooth path in  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and define the one-parameter family of paths,  $\rho^{t}(s)$ ,  $(s,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,\infty)$  by
$\rho^{t}(s)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(s)\ .$
By what has been explained above, it we can prove that
(8.10)
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\bigg|_{0+}\left(\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho^{t}(s))}\right)\leq-2\lambda\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{0}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho^{0}(s))}$
for all smooth  $\rho:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M}$  and all  $s\in(0,1)$ , we will have
proved the geodesic convexity of the relative entropy functional, and
consequently, we shall have proved
$D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho||\sigma)\leq e^{-2\lambda t}D(\rho||\sigma)\ .$
We now present a simple sufficient condition for (8.10) that we
shall be able to verify in a number of interesting examples.
8.1 DEFINITION.
A semigroup  $\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  intertwines with a semigroup
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  in case for all  $t>0$ , and all  $A\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ ,
(8.11)
$\nabla{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A=\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\nabla A\ .$
By duality, the intertwining relation  $\nabla\circ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=\vec{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}}\circ\nabla$
implies the identity
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\dive({\bf A})=\dive(\vec{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}}^{\dagger}{\bf A})\;,\qquad\text{for }{\bf A}\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}\ .$
We will be particularly interested in cases in which for some  $\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}$ ,
(8.12)
$\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}{\bf A}=(e^{-\lambda t}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A_{1},\dots,e^{-\lambda t}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ .$
8.2 Remark.
A classical example is provided by the
Mehler formula for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, which was
first studied by Mehler in 1866. For  $\beta>0$ , let
$\gamma_{\beta}(x)=(\beta/2\pi)^{n/2}e^{-\beta|x|^{2}/2}$  be the centered Gaussian density on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$  with zero mean and variance  $n/\beta$ . For  $t>0$  and bounded continuous functions  $f$  on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ , define  $P_{t}f$  by
(8.13)
$P_{t}f(x)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}f(e^{-t}x+(1-e^{-2t})^{1/2}y)\gamma_{\beta}(y)\>{\rm d}y\ .$
Then  $P_{t}$  is a classical Markov semigroup; namely the Mehler or
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. The dual semigroup  $P_{t}^{\dagger}$  acting on
probability densities  $\rho$  on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$  is defined by
$\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}P_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(x)f(x)\>{\rm d}x=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\rho(x)P_{t}f(x)\>{\rm d}x$
A change of variables yields the dual Mehler formula:
$P_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(x)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\rho\big(e^{-t}x-(1-e^{-2t})^{1/2}y\big)\gamma_{\beta}\big((1-e^{-2t})^{1/2}x+e^{-t}y\big)\>{\rm d}y\ .$
A Taylor expansion in (8.13) and then integration by parts show that
$f(x,t):=P_{t}f(x)$  and  $\rho(x,t):=P_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(x)$  satisfy
$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}f(x,t)=\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\dive-x\right)\nabla f(x,t)\quad{\rm and}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho(x,t)=\dive\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\nabla+x\right)\rho(x,t)\ .$
It is immediate from (8.13) that
(8.14)
$\nabla P_{t}f(x)=\ \vec{P}_{t}\nabla f(x)$
where  $\vec{P}_{t}(v_{1},\dots v_{n})(x)=e^{-t}(P_{t}v_{1}(x),\dots,P_{t}v_{n}(x))$ .
We shall see below that an identity similar to (8.14) is readily proved for the Fermi and Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.
Using (8.14), which is a direct analog of (8.11) and (8.12), Ledoux [44, p. 447] gave a very simple proof of the optimal logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.
A key element in his proof is the joint convexity of  $(a,r)\mapsto|a|^{2}/r$  on  ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}\times(0,\infty)$ , for which we will need a suitable non-commutative analogue.
The latter is provided by a well-known convexity inequality for matrices, which asserts that, for all  $\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , the mapping
(8.15)
$\displaystyle(\rho,A)\mapsto\langle A,[\rho]_{{\omega}}^{-1}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}={\rm Tr}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\infty}(t{{\bf 1}}+e^{-\omega/2}\rho)^{-1}A^{*}(t{{\bf 1}}+e^{\omega/2}\rho)^{-1}A\>{\rm d}t\bigg]$
is jointly convex on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}\times\mathcal{A}$ ; see [36, 37]. Note that if  $\rho$  and  $A$  are scalars, the right-hand side reduces to  $A^{2}/\rho$ .
The non-commutative convexity result ultimately derives from Lieb’s concavity Theorem [41]. Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$  is completely positive, it follows from (8.15) that
(8.16)
$\displaystyle\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A,[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho]_{{\omega}}^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\leq\langle A,[\rho]_{{\omega}}^{-1}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .$
There is a well-developed theory of monotone metrics beginning with work of Chentsov and Morozova [52] for classical Markov processes and its non-commutative extension initiated by Petz [62], and further developed in [40, 34, 60, 35, 70]. Other results from this theory will be useful in further developments.
Now consider any smooth path  $\rho:[0,1]\to{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and for each  $s\in(0,1)$  write
$\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s)=\dive{\bf A}(s)$
where  ${\bf A}(s)$  is the solution of  $\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s)=\dive{\bf A}(s)$  that minimizes
$\langle{\bf A},[\rho]_{{\vec{\omega}}}^{-1}{\bf A}\rangle_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}$  so that, by the definitions in Section 7,
$g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}(\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s),\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s))=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j}(s),[\rho(s)]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}A_{j}(s)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .$
Set  $\rho^{t}(s):={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(s)$ , and suppose that the semigroup  $\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  defined by (8.12) intertwines with  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ .
It follows that
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{t}(s)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\dive{\bf A}(s)=\dive\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}{\bf A}(s)\ .$
Consequently, by (8.12) and (8.16),
$\displaystyle\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho^{t}(s))}$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j}(s),[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(s)]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j}(s)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}$
$\displaystyle\leq$
$\displaystyle e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j}(s),[\rho(s)]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}A_{j}(s)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=e^{-2\lambda t}\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho(s))}\ ,$
which clearly implies (8.10).
Altogether we have proved:
8.3 THEOREM.
Let  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , and let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$  be an ergodic QMS that satisfies the  $\sigma$ -DBC.
Let  $\nabla$  and  $\dive$  denote the associated non-commutative gradient and divergence.
Suppose that for some  $\lambda>0$ , the semigroup  $\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  defined by (8.12) intertwines with
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ .
Then the relative entropy with respect to  $\sigma$  is geodesically  $\lambda$ -convex on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  for the Riemannian metric  $(g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho})_{\rho}$ .
Moreover, the exponential convergence estimate
$\displaystyle D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho||\sigma)\leq e^{-2\lambda t}D(\rho||\sigma)$
holds, as well as the generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality
(8.17)
$\displaystyle D(\rho||\sigma)\leq\frac{1}{2\lambda}\tau\big[-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\rho)\big(\log\rho-\log\sigma\big)\big]\ .$
While it is a problem of ongoing research to extend Theorem 8.3 to the infinite dimensional setting, the part of it concerning entropy and entropy production inequalities is relatively robust, as it relies most essentially on Lieb’s convexity result, while the part of it concerning geodesic convexity is more involved and requires more work to generalize. Therefore, with regard to the infinite dimensional Bose-Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, we are not presently in a positions to make any statements about geodesic convexity of the entropy, but the situation is much better concerning entropy and entropy production.
Let  $\mathcal{D}[\rho]=\tau\big[-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\rho)\big(\log\rho-\log\sigma\big)\big]$  be the entropy dissipation functional, which is minus the derivative of
$D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho||\sigma)$  at  $t=0$ . By Theorem 5.10,
$-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\Big)={\rm div}({\bf A})\ .$
The entropy dissipation functional  $\mathcal{D}[\rho]$  is then given by
$\mathcal{D}[\rho]=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j},[\rho]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}A_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .$
Now replace  $\rho$  by  $\rho(t):={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho$  and let us assume that  $\rho$  is in the domain of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}$ , a trivial assumption in the finite dimensional case. Then
$\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t}\rho(t)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}({\rm div}({\bf A}))\ ,$
and assuming that  $\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  defined by (8.12) intertwines with  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ , we have that
${\bf A}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{1},\dots,{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ .$
Therefore, by the convexity argument used in the proof of Theorem 8.3
$\mathcal{D}[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho]=e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j},[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\leq e^{-2\lambda t}\mathcal{D}[\rho]\ .$
By a standard argument, the generalized log-Sobolev inequality (8.17) follows immediately for  $\rho$  in the domain of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}$ .
In summary, if one is interested more in entropy dissipation inequalities than the geodesic convexity of the entropy Theorem 5.10
together with an intertwining relation allows one to bypass the Riemannian structure. This fact also underlines the utility of writing the evolution equation as gradient flow for the entropy, which is essential for the argument.
In the rest of this section we explain how intertwining formulas may be proved. We consider two examples, already introduced, namely the Bose and Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups. In the Fermi case, we are within the scope of the finite dimensional picture developed here, and we will be able to prove the geodesic convexity of the relative entropy. In the Bose case, we are in an infinite dimensional setting, and work remains to be done to rigorously prove the geodesic convexity in this case. However, by what has been explained in the preceding paragraphs, we shall obtain a rigorously valid generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality.
8.2. Intertwining via commutation formulas
For both the Fermi and Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ , there is a
Mehler type formula for
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  from which the intertwining can be readily checked. In the Fermi case,
this can be found in formulas (4.1) and (4.2) of [11], and the formula in the Bose case is a simple adaptation of this.
Fortunately however, it is not necessary to find an explicit formula for the action of
the semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  to prove the intertwining identity and (8.12). In case where such identities are true, they can often be readily checked using the form of the generator  ${{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ .
8.4 LEMMA.
Suppose that for some numbers  $a_{j}$ ,  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ ,
(8.18)
$\displaystyle[\partial_{j},{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}]=-a_{j}\partial_{j}\ $
for each  $j\in{\mathcal{J}}$ . Then defining  $\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}$  by
$\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})=(e^{-ta_{1}}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A_{1},\dots,e^{-ta_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ ,$
we have the intertwining relation  $\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\partial_{j}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$ .
Proof.
Let  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  and define  $A(t)=\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A$ . Then  $A(0)=\partial_{j}A$  and
$\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}A(t)=\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A-a_{j}\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A=[{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}-a_{j}I]A(t)\ .$
It follows that  $t\mapsto e^{ta_{j}}A(t)$  is the unique solution of
${\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}X(t)={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}X(t)}$  with
$X(0)=\partial_{j}A$ , which is of course  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\partial_{j}A$ . Therefore,
$\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A=e^{-ta_{j}}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\partial_{j}A$ .
∎
8.5 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  be the Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with generator
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$  given in (6.17), and let  $\sigma_{\beta}$  be its invariant state. Then for all  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ ,
$D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\rho||\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-2\sinh(\beta/2)t}D(\rho||\sigma_{\beta})\ .$
Proof.
Using (6.18), we may apply Lemma 8.4, and then the remarks following Theorem 8.3. (Note that for all  $t>0$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}$  is in the domain of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}$  so that the generalized log-Sobolev inequality is valid.)
∎
Results in [38, Appendix D] show that the constant  $2\sinh(\beta/2)$  in Theorem 8.5 cannot be improved.
We may make a similar application of Lemma 8.4, and then Theorem 8.3 itself to the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.
However, in this case, it is not the differential structure in terms of the derivations  $\partial_{j}$  for which we have (8.18), but the skew derivations  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  and  $\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$ .
This was proved in (6.13) and (6.14).
However, the metric can be written in terms of  ${{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  and  $\overline{{{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.12962pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.12962pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.43518pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.43518pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.8611pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.9371pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.97221pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.97221pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.47221pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=5.41144pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial$}\crcr}}}}}}}_{j}$
$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.94444pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.97566pt}$  just as well, bringing in the principle automorphism  $\Gamma$ , and indeed, this is how the metric was written in [12].
This permits us to argue as above in the Bose case, and we conclude:
8.6 THEOREM.
For  $\beta\geq 0$ , let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  be the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with generator
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$  given in (6.8), and let  $\sigma_{\beta}$  be its invariant state. Then for all  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ ,
$D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\rho||\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-2\lambda_{\beta}t}D(\rho||\sigma_{\beta})$
where
$\lambda_{\beta}=\min\{\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)\ :\ j=1,\dots,m\}$ . Moreover, the realtive entropy functional  $\rho\mapsto D(\rho||\sigma_{\beta})$
is geodesically  $\lambda_{\beta}$  convex in the Riemannain metric associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}$ .
8.3. Talagrand type inequalities
Our final results in this section extend a result from outr earlier paper [12] to the present more generla setting.
The proof is step-for-step the one from our previous paper, with only minor modifications, and we shall thereofre be brief.
However, it is worth recording the more general result since this subject has recently attracted the attention of other researchers [43, 63].
The connection between logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and transport inequalities of Talagrand type [69] was originally discovered and developed by Otto and Villani [56]. The fact that a Talgrand type inequlaity holds for our transport metric is further evidence that it is indeed a bona-fide transport metric.
8.7 THEOREM (Talagrand type inequality).
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be the generator of an ergodic QMS that satisifes the  $\sigma$ -DBC
with respect to  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ . Suppose that the generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality
(8.17) is valid for some  $\lambda>0$ .
Let  $d(\rho_{1},\rho_{2})$  denote the Riemannain distance on  ${\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  associated to  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ . For all  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ ,
(8.19)
$d(\rho,\sigma)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2D(\rho||\sigma)}{\lambda}}\ .$
Proof.
Given  $\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , define
$\rho(t)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\rho$
for  $t\in(0,\infty)$ .
Since  $\lim_{t\to\infty}\rho(t)=\sigma$ , it follows that
$d(\rho,\sigma)\leq{\rm arclength}[\rho(\cdot)]=\int_{0}^{\infty}\sqrt{g_{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))}\>{\rm d}t\ .$
Since the evolution described by  $t\mapsto{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho$  is gradient flow for the relative entropy,
${\displaystyle g_{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))=-\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm dt}}D(\rho(t)||\sigma)}$
so that
for any  $0\leq t_{1}<t_{2}<\infty$ ,
(8.20)
$\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\sqrt{g_{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))}\>{\rm d}t\leq\sqrt{t_{2}-t_{1}}\sqrt{D(\rho(t_{1})||\sigma)-D(\rho(t_{2})||\sigma)}\ .$
Fix any  $\epsilon>0$ . Define the sequence of times  $\{t_{k}\}$ ,  $k\in{\mathord{\mathbb{N}}}$ ,
$D(\rho(t_{k})||\sigma)=e^{-k\epsilon}D(\rho||\sigma)\ .$
(Since  $t\mapsto D(\rho(t)||\sigma)$  is strictly decreasing,  $t_{k}$  is well defined.)
Since  $D(\rho(t)||\sigma)\leq e^{-2\lambda t}D(\rho||\sigma)$ , for each  $k$ ,
$t_{k}-t_{k-1}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2\lambda}\ .$
Then by (8.20), with this choice of  $\{t_{k}\}$ ,
$\displaystyle\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_{k}}\sqrt{g_{\rho(t)}{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))}\>{\rm d}t$
$\displaystyle\ \leq\ \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{2\lambda}(e^{-(k-1)\epsilon}-e^{-k\epsilon}){D(\rho||\sigma)}}$
$\displaystyle\ =\ \sqrt{\frac{D(\rho||\sigma)}{2\lambda}}e^{-k\epsilon/2}\sqrt{\epsilon(e^{\epsilon}-1)}\ .$
Since
$\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}e^{-k\epsilon/2}\sqrt{\epsilon(e^{\epsilon}-1)}\right)=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}e^{-k\epsilon/2}\epsilon\right)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x/2}\>{\rm d}x=2\ ,$
we obtain the desired bound.
∎
Appendix A Proof of Theorem 3.1
In this appendix we present a simple and self-contained proof of Theorem 3.1.
The starting point is an isometry that is crucial to the characterization of quantum Markov semigroup generators given by Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudarshan [31]:
For any finite dimensional Hilbert space  ${\mathfrak{H}}$ , let  ${\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}})$  denote the linear operators from  ${\mathfrak{H}}$  to  ${\mathfrak{H}}$
equipped with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product  $\langle A,B\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}})}=({\rm dim}(\mathcal{H}))^{-1}{\rm Tr}[A^{*}B]$
so that  $\|{{\bf 1}}\|_{{\mathfrak{H}}}=1$ . As above, we use  $\dagger$  for the Hermitian adjoint in  ${\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}})$ . A special case deserves a special notation: let  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  denote the  $n\times n$  complex
matrices  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  equipped with this same normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product.
A particular orthonormal basis in  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  plays a distinguished role in what follows: For  $1\leq i,j\leq n$ , let  $E_{i,j}$
denote the  $n\times n$  matrix whose  $i,j$  entry is  $1$ , and whose other entries are all  $0$ . If  $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}$  is the standard basis of  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ , then  $E_{i,j}$  is the rank one operator that is written as  $|e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}|$  in a standard quantum mechanical notation introduced before. In this notation, one has
(A.1)
$E_{i,j}\otimes E_{i,j}=(|e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}|)\otimes(|e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}|)=|e_{i}\otimes e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}\otimes e_{j}|\ .$
It follows that
(A.2)
$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}E_{i,j}\otimes E_{i,j}=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|\quad{\rm where}\quad\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}e_{j}\otimes e_{j}$
is a rank one projection in  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ , and, in particular, is positive. This observation is due to Choi, and some of the simple but fundamental conclusions he drew from it are related below. More immediately,  $\{E_{i,j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$  is an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  called the matrix unit basis.
There is a natural identification of  ${\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})$  with
${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  that takes advantage of the multiplication on
${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ : For  $A,B\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ , define
the operator  $\#(A\otimes B):{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  by
$\#(A\otimes B):\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\to\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\ ,\qquad\#(A\otimes B)X=AXB\ ,$
for all  $X\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ . It follows that the adjoint of  $\#(A\otimes B)$  as an operator on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  is given by
$\big(\#(A\otimes B)\big)^{\dagger}=\#(A^{*}\otimes B^{*})$ .
Moreover,
(A.3)
$\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\#(A\otimes B)]={\rm Tr}[A]{\rm Tr}[B]\ .$
The left-hand side of (A.3) involves the trace for operators on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ , whereas the right-hand side involves the trace for operators on  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ .
A.1 LEMMA.
Let  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  and  $\{G_{\beta}\}$  be two orthonormal bases of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ , so that  $\{F_{\alpha}\otimes G_{\beta}\}$  is an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ .
Then  $\{\#(F_{\alpha}\otimes G_{\beta})\}$  is orthonormal in  ${\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})$ .
In particular, the map  $\#$  is unitary from  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  into  ${\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})$ .
Proof of Lemma A.1.
We may compute the trace on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  using
any orthonormal basis, and
using the matrix unit orthonormal basis  $\{E_{i,j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$ , we have
for all  $\alpha,\beta$  and  $\mu,\nu$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle\#(F_{\alpha}\otimes G_{\beta}),\#(F_{\mu}\otimes G_{\nu})\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}(\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}))}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle n^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}{\rm Tr}[(F_{\alpha}E_{i,j}G_{\beta})^{*}F_{\mu}E_{i,j}G_{\nu}]$
$\displaystyle=n^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}{\rm Tr}[G_{\beta}^{*}E_{j,i}F_{\alpha}^{*}F_{\mu}E_{i,j}G_{\nu}]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle n^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}(G_{\nu}G_{\beta}^{*})_{j,j}(F_{\alpha}^{*}F_{\mu})_{i,i}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle n^{-1}{\rm Tr}[G_{\nu}G_{\beta}^{*}]n^{-1}{\rm Tr}[F_{\alpha}^{*}F_{\mu}]=\delta_{\alpha,\mu}\delta_{\beta,\nu}\ .$
∎
Consider any linear transformation  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , and hence on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ . Let
$\{F_{\beta}\}$  be any orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ .
Then  $\{F_{\alpha}^{*}\}$  is also an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ , and by
Lemma A.1,  $\{\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta})\}$
is an orthonormal basis of  ${\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})$ . Thus  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  has the expansion
(A.4)
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta})\ .$
or, what is the same,
(A.5)
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\qquad{\rm for\ all}\ A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\ ,$
where the coefficients  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  are given by
(A.6)
$c_{\alpha,\beta}=\langle\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta}),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}\ .$
This orthonormal expansion is fundamental to the work of Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudarshan on the structure of generators of quantum Markov semigroups.
A.2 DEFINITION.
The  $n^{2}\times n^{2}$  matrix  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  with entries given by (A.6) is called the
GKS matrix for the operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with respect to the orthonormal basis
$\{F_{\alpha}\}$ . When we wish to emphasize the dependence on  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$ , we write  $c_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$ .
A.3 Remark.
Let  $A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  and consider the case  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}=\#(A\otimes B)$ . By the isometry proved in Lemma A.1, the GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is given by
$\displaystyle c_{\alpha,\beta}$
$\displaystyle=\langle\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta}),\#(A\otimes B)\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}=\langle F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta},A\otimes B\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}}$
$\displaystyle=n^{-2}{\rm Tr}[F_{\alpha}A]{\rm Tr}[F^{*}_{\beta}B]\ .$
In particular, the identity transformation on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  results from the choice  $A=B={{\bf 1}}$ , and so the GKS matrix of the identity transformation is the rank-one matrix
(A.7)
$c_{\alpha,\beta}=n^{-2}{\rm Tr}[F_{\alpha}]{\rm Tr}[F^{*}_{\beta}]\ .$
This formula will be useful later on.
The following lemma is from [31]; for the convenience of the reader we give a short proof.
A.4 LEMMA.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  be a linear operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , and let
$\{F_{\alpha}\}$  be an orthonormal basis of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Then the GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with respect to  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  is self-adjoint if and only if  $({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*}$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Proof.
Write  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  as in (A.4) and define  $\widetilde{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A):=({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*})^{*}$ . Then
$\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)=\Big(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}A^{*}F_{\beta}\Big)^{*}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{c_{\alpha,\beta}}F_{\beta}^{*}AF_{\alpha}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{c_{\beta,\alpha}}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\ .$
By the uniqueness of the expansion (A.4),  $\tilde{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  if and only if
$c_{\alpha,\beta}=\overline{c_{\beta,\alpha}}$  for all  $\alpha,\beta$ .
∎
The GKS matrix of a linear transformation  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  from  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  to  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  is closely related to the Choi matrix
of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$ . Let  $\{E_{i,j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$  be matrix unit basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ .
The Choi matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is the element of  $\mathcal{M}_{n^{2}}({\mathbb{C}})$
(A.8)
$C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})\otimes E_{i,j}\ ,$
viewed as the  $n\times n$  block matrix with entries in  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  whose  $i,j$  entry is  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})$ .
If we now identify  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{n}$  with  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  by identifying  $v\otimes w$  with  $\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}v_{i}w_{j}E_{i,j}$ ,
$C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$  becomes an operator on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ .
The identity provided by the following lemma was pointed out in [58], and used there to simplify part of the proof [31] of their theorem on the structure of generators of quantum Markov semigroups on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
A.5 LEMMA.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  be a linear operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , and let  $C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$  be defined by (A.8).
Identify  ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{n}$  with  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  by identifying  $v\otimes w$  with  $\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}v_{i}w_{j}E_{i,j}$ , so that
$C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$  is identified with an operator on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ . Then for all  $F,G\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ ,
(A.9)
$\langle G,C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})F\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}}=\langle\#(G\otimes F^{*}),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}$
Proof.
By direct computation,
$\displaystyle\langle G,C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})F\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell,m,p=1}^{n}\overline{G}_{k,m}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}[E_{i,j}]_{m,p}F_{\ell,p}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell,m,p=1}^{n}F_{\ell,p}[E_{j,i}]_{p,m}\overline{G}_{k,m}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}(FE_{j,i}G^{*})_{\ell,k}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}(GE_{i,j}F^{*})^{*}_{\ell,k}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}=\langle\#(G\otimes F^{*}),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}\ .$
∎
A fundamental theorem of Choi [15] says that a linear transformation  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  is
completely positive if and only if its Choi matrix  $C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$  is positive as an operator on  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ . Indeed, in the notation of (A.2)
$C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})=n{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\otimes{{\bf 1}}_{\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})}\left(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|\right)\ ,$
Hence, when  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is completely positive,  $C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$  is positive. The converse is also true:
Choi used an elementary spectral decomposition [15] to show that when  $C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})$  is positive,
then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is completely positive.
A.6 Remark.
The identity (A.9) shows that if  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  is any orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$ , then the GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with respect to this basis is positive if and only if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is completely positive. In other words, the GKS representation (A.5) of a linear operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$
is well-suited to the question of whether  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is completely positive or not.
Going forward, it will be convenient to assume that our orthonormal bases  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  are indexed by
$\alpha\in\{1,\dots,n\}\times\{1,\dots,n\}$ , and we write  $\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})$ . For such bases, we make the following definition:
A.7 DEFINITION.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be an operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  such that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$  and
$({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A^{*}$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}$ .
Let  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  be any orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  such that
$F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}$ . Let  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  be the GKS matrix for
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with respect to  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$ .
The  $(n^{2}-1)\times(n^{2}-1)$  matrix with entries  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  where
$\alpha$  and  $\beta$  range over the set
$\{(i,j)\ :\ 1\leq i,j\leq n\quad{\rm and}\quad(i,j)\neq(1,1)\}$  is called the reduced GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  for the basis  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$ .
The following lemma is due to Parravinci and Zecca [58]:
A.8 LEMMA.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be a linear operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , and let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ . Let  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  be an orthonormal basis for  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  with  $F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}$ . Let  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  be the GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with respect to  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$ . Then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is completely positive for all  $t\geq 0$  if and only if the reduced GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is positive.
Proof.
Suppose that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is completely positive for each  $t>0$ . By (A.7), the GKS matrix of the identity transformation is
(A.10)
$c_{\alpha,\beta}(I)=\delta_{\alpha,(1,1)}\delta_{\beta,(1,1)}\ .$
In particular, the reduced GKS matrix of the identity is zero.
Then since
$c_{\alpha,\beta}(t^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-I))=t^{-1}c_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t})-t^{-1}c_{\alpha,\beta}(I)\ ,$
it follows that the reduced GKS matrix of  $t^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-I)$  coincides with the reduced GKS matrix of
$t^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ , and by Remark A.6 this is positive. Taking the limit  $t\to 0$ , we conclude that the reduced GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is positive.
Conversely, suppose that the reduced GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is positive. For small  $t>0$ ,
$c_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t})=c_{\alpha,\beta}(I)+tc_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}})+o(t)$
By (A.10), this is positive for all sufficiently small  $t$ . By Remark A.6,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is completely positive for all sufficiently small  $t>0$ .
Then by the semigroup property,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is completely positive for all  $t>0$ .
∎
We now temporarily put aside complete positivity, and consider a linear transformation  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$
such that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  preserves self-adjointness, and such that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$ .
A.9 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be a linear operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  such that
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$  and  $({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A^{*}$  for all  $A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}$ .
Let  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  be any orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  such that  $F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}$ .
Let  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  be the GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  for  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$ .
Then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is given by
(A.11)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=-i[H,A]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}\left(F_{\alpha}^{*}[A,F_{\beta}]+[F^{*}_{\alpha},A]F_{\beta}\right)$
where  $H$  is the traceless self-adjoint matrix given by
(A.12)
$H=\frac{1}{2i}\sum_{\beta\neq(1,1)}(c_{(1,1),\beta}F_{\beta}-c_{\beta,(1,1)}F^{*}_{\beta})\ .$
Notice that only the reduced GKS matrix figures in the second term on the right
in (A.11).
Proof of Theorem A.9.
Let
$c_{\alpha,\beta}$  be the GKS matrix for  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with respect to  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  where  $F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}$ .
Then by Lemma A.4,  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  is a self-adjoint matrix.
By (A.5), for all  $A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ ,
(A.13)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}=G^{*}A+AG+\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}$
where
${\displaystyle G=\frac{c_{(1,1),(1,1)}}{2}{{\bf 1}}+\sum_{\beta\neq(1,1)}c_{(1,1),\beta}F_{\beta}}$ .
Let  $K=\frac{1}{2}(G+G^{*})$  and  $H=\frac{1}{2i}(G-G^{*})$  be the self-adjoint matrices such that  $G=K+iH$ .
Then (A.13) becomes
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=-i[H,A]+KA+AK+\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\ .$
Then  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$  implies
${\displaystyle K=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}F^{*}_{\alpha}F_{\beta}}$ ,
and thus, for all  $A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ ,
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-i[H,A]+\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}\left(F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}-\frac{1}{2}F^{*}_{\alpha}F_{\beta}A-\frac{1}{2}AF^{*}_{\alpha}F_{\beta}\right)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-i[H,A]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}\left(F_{\alpha}^{*}[A,F_{\beta}]+[F^{*}_{\alpha},A]F_{\beta}\right)\ .$
Since  ${\rm Tr}[G]=\tfrac{n}{2}c_{(1.1),(1,1)}\in{\mathbb{R}}$ , and  ${\rm Tr}[H]$  is the imaginary part of  ${\rm Tr}[G]$ , it follows that  ${\rm Tr}[H]=0$ .
∎
A.10 THEOREM.
Let  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  be the generator of a QMS that is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  for some  $s\in[0,1]$ ,  $s\neq 1/2$ . Let  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  be the GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with
respect to a modular orthonormal basis of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  defined in Definition 1.2.
Then for all  $\alpha,\beta$ ,
(A.14)
$e^{\omega_{\alpha}}c_{\alpha,\beta}=c_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega_{\beta}}\ ,$
and
(A.15)
$c_{\alpha,\beta}=e^{-\omega_{\alpha}}c_{\beta^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}}\ ,$
where the  $\omega_{\alpha}$  are defined in (3.1).
In particular,  $c$  commutes with the diagonal matrix
$[\delta_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega\beta}]$ , so that the eigenspaces of the latter are eigenspaces of  $c$ .
A.11 Remark.
The conditions (A.14) and (A.15)
are independent of  $s$ . Furthermore, (A.14) implies that
(A.16)
$\omega_{\alpha}\neq\omega_{\beta}\quad\Rightarrow\quad c_{\alpha,\beta}=0\ .$
Therefore with an ordering of the indices  $\alpha$  so that
$\alpha\geq\beta\iff\omega_{\alpha}\geq\omega_{\beta}$ , the matrix
$[c_{\alpha,\beta}]$  is block-diagonal.
Proof of Theorem A.10.
Since  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  preserves self-adjointness and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$ .
Thus, for any orthonormal basis  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  of  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{n}$  such that  $F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}$ , Theorem A.9 applies.
We now fix such a basis and focus on the additional consequences of
self-adjointness with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$ .
By Lemma 2.5,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  commutes with the modular group, and this means that for all  $A$ ,
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sigma^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(\sigma A\sigma^{-1}))\sigma\ .$
In terms of the GKS expansion for  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ , and making use of (3.2),
$\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sigma^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(\sigma A\sigma^{-1}))\sigma=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}\sigma^{-1}F_{\alpha}^{*}\sigma A\sigma^{-1}F_{\beta}\sigma$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega_{\beta}-\omega_{\alpha}}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\ .$
Now (A.14) follows from the uniqueness of the coefficients.
To prove (A.15), note that for any  $A,B$ ,
${\rm Tr}[B^{*}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A]=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}{\rm Tr}[B^{*}c_{\alpha,\beta}F^{*}_{\alpha}AF_{\beta}]=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}{\rm Tr}[c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\beta}B^{*}F^{*}_{\alpha}A]=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}{\rm Tr}[(\overline{c_{\alpha,\beta}}F_{\alpha}BF^{*}_{\beta})^{*}A]\ .$
Using Lemma A.4 we conclude that
${\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}B=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{c_{\alpha,\beta}}F_{\alpha}BF^{*}_{\beta}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\beta,\alpha}F_{\alpha}BF^{*}_{\beta}}$ .
Then
$\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A,B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A))^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s}]=\\
{\rm Tr}[A^{*}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s})]=\langle A,\sigma^{s-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s})\sigma^{-s}\rangle_{s}\ .$
The self-adjointness of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  with respect to  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}$  then yields
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(B)=\sigma^{s-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s})\sigma^{-s}$
for all  $B$ . Using the GKS expansion for a modular basis and (3.2),
$\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}BF_{\beta}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\beta,\alpha}\sigma^{s-1}F_{\alpha}\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s}F_{\beta}^{*}\sigma^{-s}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\beta,\alpha}e^{(1-s)\omega_{\alpha}}e^{s\omega_{\beta}}F_{\alpha}BF_{\beta}^{*}\ .$
Since  $F_{\gamma}^{*}=F_{\gamma^{\prime}}$  and  $\omega_{\gamma}=-\omega_{\gamma^{\prime}}$  for all  $\gamma$ , we can rewrite this as
$\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}BF_{\beta}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\beta^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}}e^{(s-1)\omega_{\alpha}}e^{-s\omega_{\beta}}F_{\alpha}^{*}BF_{\beta}\ .$
By the uniqueness of the coefficients, it follows that  $e^{-s\omega_{\alpha}}c_{\alpha,\beta}e^{s\omega_{\beta}}=e^{-\omega_{\alpha}}c_{\beta^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}}$  for all  $\alpha,\beta$ .
However, by (A.14),  $c$  commutes with the  $s$ th power of
$[\delta_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega_{\alpha}}]$ , and thus
$e^{-s\omega_{\alpha}}c_{\alpha,\beta}e^{s\omega_{\beta}}=c_{\alpha,\beta}$ .
This proves (A.15).
∎
Proof of Theorem 3.1.
By assumption  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  has an extension  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  from  ${\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}$  to a QMS on all of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ . It suffices to treat  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ , and to simplify the notation we assume the extension is done and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is a QMS on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Let  $\{F_{\alpha}\}$  be a modular basis for  $\sigma$ , and consider the GKS expansion
(A.17)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\ .$
By Theorem A.9, we can rewrite (A.17) as
(A.18)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=-i[H,A]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}\left(F_{\alpha}^{*}[A,F_{\beta}]+[F^{*}_{\alpha},A]F_{\beta}\right)\ ,\ $
where by (A.16), (A.12) reduces to
$\displaystyle H$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2i\sqrt{n}}\sum_{\beta\neq(1,1),\ \omega_{\beta}=0}(c_{(1,1),\beta}F_{\beta}-c_{\beta,(1,1)}F^{*}_{\beta})$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2i\sqrt{n}}\sum_{\beta\neq(1,1),\ \omega_{\beta}=0}(c_{(1,1),\beta}-c_{\beta^{\prime},(1,1)})F_{\beta}\ .$
By (A.15) and (A.16),
$c_{(1,1),\beta}=c_{\beta^{\prime},(1,1)}$ , and therefore  $H=0$ .
Making use of the fact that for all  $\gamma$ ,  $F_{\gamma}^{*}=F_{\gamma^{\prime}}$ ,
we replace  $\alpha$  with
$\beta^{\prime}$  and  $\beta$  with  $\alpha^{\prime}$  and use (A.15) to rewrite (A.17) as
(A.19)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha^{\prime}}AF^{*}_{\beta^{\prime}}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\beta^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}}F_{\beta}AF^{*}_{\alpha}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega_{\alpha}}F_{\beta}AF^{*}_{\alpha}\ .$
By Theorem A.9, we can rewrite (A.19) as
(A.20)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=-i[\widehat{H},A]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\ \neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega_{\alpha}}\left(F_{\beta}[A,F_{\alpha}^{*}]+[F_{\beta},A]F^{*}_{\alpha}\right)\ $
By (A.16), (A.12) reduces to
${\displaystyle\widehat{H}=\frac{1}{2i\sqrt{n}}\sum_{\alpha\neq(1,1),\ \omega_{\alpha}=0}(c_{(1,1),\alpha}F^{*}_{\alpha}-c_{\alpha,(1,1)}F_{\alpha})}$ . The same argument that led to
$H=0$  leads to  $\widehat{H}=0$ .
Averaging (A.18) and (A.20), taking into account  $H=\widehat{H}=0$ , we obtain
(A.21)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\neq(1,1)}c_{\alpha,\beta}[\left(F_{\alpha}^{*}[A,F_{\beta}]+[F^{*}_{\alpha},A]F_{\beta}\right)+e^{\omega_{\alpha}}\left(F_{\beta}[A,F_{\alpha}^{*}]+[F_{\beta},A]F^{*}_{\alpha}\right)]\ .$
Now let  $U$  be an  $(n^{2}-1)\times(n^{2}-1)$  unitary matrix that diagonalizes the reduced
GKS matrix  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  and which commutes with the matrix
$\delta_{\alpha,\beta}e^{\omega_{\alpha}}$ ,  $\alpha,\beta\neq(1,1)$  so that  $U_{\gamma,\alpha}=0$
unless  $\omega_{\gamma}=\omega_{\alpha}$ .
We may then write
(A.22)
$c_{\alpha,\beta}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma\neq(1,1)}U^{*}_{\alpha,\gamma}e^{-\omega_{\gamma}/2}c_{\gamma}U_{\gamma,\beta}$
Each  $c_{\gamma}$  is non-negative since, by Lemma A.8 the reduced
GKS matrix  $c_{\alpha,\beta}$  is positive, and since
$U_{\gamma,\alpha}=0$  unless  $\omega_{\gamma}=\omega_{\alpha}$ ,
we also have  ${\displaystyle e^{\omega_{\alpha}}c_{\alpha,\beta}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma}U^{*}_{\alpha,\gamma}e^{\omega_{\gamma}/2}c_{\gamma}U_{\gamma,\beta}}$ .
Defining  $V_{\gamma}=\sum_{\beta}U_{\gamma,\beta}F_{\beta}$ ,
we may rewrite (A.21) as
(A.23)
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\gamma\neq(1,1)}c_{\gamma}[e^{-\omega_{\gamma}/2}\left(V_{\gamma}^{*}[A,V_{\gamma}]+[V^{*}_{\gamma},A]V_{\gamma}\right)+e^{\omega_{\gamma}/2}\left(V_{\gamma}[A,V_{\gamma}^{*}]+[V_{\gamma},A]V_{\gamma}^{*}\right)]\ .$
By symmetry, we may assume without loss of generality that  $c_{\gamma}=c_{\gamma^{\prime}}$  where
as before  $(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})^{\prime}=(\gamma_{2},\gamma_{1})$  so that  $V_{\gamma}^{*}=V_{\gamma^{\prime}}$ .
Then the expression simplifies to
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sum_{\gamma\neq(1,1)}c_{\gamma}[e^{-\omega_{\gamma}/2}V_{\gamma}^{*}[A,V_{\gamma}]+e^{\omega_{\gamma}/2}[V_{\gamma},A]V_{\gamma}^{*}]$
which is (3.3).
Simply using (A.22) directly in (A.18) leads to the alternate form
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=\sum_{\gamma\neq(1,1)}c_{\gamma}e^{-\omega_{\gamma}/2}\left(V_{\gamma}^{*}[A,V_{\gamma}]+[V^{*}_{\gamma},A]V_{\gamma}\right)\ .$
Again since  $U_{\gamma,\alpha}=0$  unless
$\omega_{\gamma}=\omega_{\alpha}$ , (3.2) implies that
for all  $\gamma$  and all  $t$ ,
(A.24)
$\sigma^{t}V_{\gamma}\sigma^{-t}=e^{-t\omega_{\gamma}}V_{\gamma}$
Letting  ${\mathcal{J}}=\{(k,\ell)\,:\,1\leq k,\ell,\leq n\quad{\rm and}\quad(k,\ell)\neq(1,1)\ \}$ ,
we see that under the hypotheses of the theorem,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  must have the form (3.3), and
(3.5) is the differential statement of (A.23).
The final step is to absorb the  $c_{j}$ ’s nto the  $V_{j}$ ’s: Since  $c_{j}\geq 0$  for each  $j$ , we can absorb these by
by making the replacement  $V_{j}\to\sqrt{c_{j}}V_{j}$ . This proves that the generator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  of a QMS satisfying the  $\sigma$ -DBC has the from specified in Theorem 3.1.
For the converse, if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  has the specified form, one restores the  $c_{j}$ ’s by normalizing the  $V_{j}$ ’s, and then writes
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  in its GKS form for this orthonormal basis (after including  ${{\bf 1}}$  and any  $V_{j}$ ’s with  $c_{j}=0$ ). The reduced
GKS matrix of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is unchanged as the argument starting from (A.13) shows. Thus, by Remark A.6,
${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  generates a completely positive semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$ , and evidently  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$ , so that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is a QMS. The
$\sigma$ -DBC is then readily checked (using the fact that the  $V_{j}$  are eigenvectors of  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ ).
∎
A.12 Remark.
It is easy to check the existence of an extension of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  from  ${\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}$  to  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  in many relevant cases; e.g., when  ${\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}$  is a Clifford algebra with an odd number of generators. One might hope that
there is a general extension using the conditional expectation.
Recall that for any unital  $C^{*}$ -subalgebra  $\mathcal{A}$  of  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , there is the conditional expectation  $E_{\mathcal{A}}$  which is the orthogonal projection in  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})}$  onto  ${\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}$  [72]. This may be written as an average over the unitaries in the commutant of  $\mathcal{A}$  [10, 71]; the connected component of this group  $\mathfrak{U}$  that contains the identity is a Lie subgroup of  $SU(n)$ , on which there exists a normalized Haar measure  $\mu$ , and then for all  $X\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ ,
${\displaystyle E_{\mathcal{A}}X=\int_{\mathfrak{U}}U^{*}XU{\rm d}\mu}(U)$ .
Evidently,  $E_{\mathcal{A}}$  is a completely positive map with  $E_{\mathcal{A}}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}$ .
That is,  $E_{\mathcal{A}}$  is a quantum Markov operator.
If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is a linear transformation on  $\mathcal{A}$ , define a linear transformation  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  by  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\circ E_{\mathcal{A}}$ .
Note that when a linear operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  is completely positive, so is  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$ , and the
restriction of  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$  to  $\mathcal{A}$  is simply  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}$ .
Moreover, if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{1}$  and  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{2}$  are two linear transformations of  $\mathcal{A}$ , then  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{2}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{1}=\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{2}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{1}}$ .
In this way we can “lift” any QMS  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  on  $\mathcal{A}$  up to a one-parameter family of Markov operators  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  such that for all  $s,t\geq 0$ ,  $\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}}\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{s}}=\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t+s}}$ .
This construction fails to yield a semigroup only because  $\lim_{t\to 0}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=E_{\mathcal{A}}$
and not  $\lim_{t\to 0}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=I_{\mathcal{A}}$ .
However, if  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ , then  ${\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-E_{\mathcal{A}})=\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}$ .
The operator  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is evidently a self-adjointness preserving linear transformation from
$\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  to  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ , and  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0$ . If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  satisfies the
$\sigma$ -DBC for  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A})$ , then for all  $A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ ,
$\tau[\sigma B^{*}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A]=\tau[\sigma B^{*}E_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(E_{\mathcal{A}}A)]=\tau[(E_{\mathcal{A}}(B\sigma)^{*}){\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(E_{\mathcal{A}}A)]=\tau[\sigma(E_{\mathcal{A}}B)^{*}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(E_{\mathcal{A}}A)]\ ,$
where we have used the fact that since  $\sigma\in\mathcal{A}$ ,  $E_{\mathcal{A}}(\sigma B^{*})=\sigma E_{\mathcal{A}}B^{*}$ . It follows
that for each  $t\geq 0$ ,  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the  $\sigma$ -GNS inner product
on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ . Consequently, the same is true of  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$ .
Therefore, the proof of Theorem 3.1 given just above shows that  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  has the form specified in Theorem 3.1 except that some  $c_{j}$ ’s might be negative: Applicability of Lemma A.8 requires that  $\lim_{t\to 0}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=I_{\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})}$ .
Appendix B Note on KMS-symmetry
We give a construction of a class of operators  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  that satisfy
$({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*}$  for all  $A$  and that are self-adjoint with respect to the  $\sigma$ -KMS inner product  $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}$  for some  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ , but which do not commute with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ , and consequently are not self-adjoint with respect to the  $\sigma$ -GNS inner product.
An operator  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  that is self-adjoint with respect to
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}$  for some  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  is called KMS-symmetric.
When  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is completely positive with  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}({{\bf 1}})={{\bf 1}}$ , it has a Kraus representation
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}K_{j}^{*}AK_{j}\quad{\rm where}\quad\sum_{j=1}^{m}K^{*}_{j}K_{j}={{\bf 1}}\ $
for some set  $\{K_{1},\dots,K_{m}\}\subset\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ . Evidently,
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}A=\sum_{j=1}^{m}K_{j}AK_{j}^{*}$ . Suppose that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma$
with  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$ . The dual set of Kraus operators
$\{\widehat{K}_{1},\dots,\widehat{K}_{m}\}$  is given by
$\widehat{K}_{j}=\Delta^{1/2}_{\sigma}K_{j}^{*}=\sigma^{1/2}K_{j}^{*}\sigma^{-1/2}\ .$
Then
${\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\widehat{K}^{*}_{j}\widehat{K}_{j}={{\bf 1}}}$  and
$\displaystyle{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\widehat{K}_{j}\sigma\widehat{K}_{j}^{*}=\sigma}$ .
It follows that the operator  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  defined by
${\displaystyle\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\widehat{K}^{*}_{j}A\widehat{K}_{j}}$  is completely positive with  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}({{\bf 1}})={{\bf 1}}$  and
${{\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}}}}\,\mbox{}^{\dagger}(\sigma)=\sigma$ .
A simple calculation shows that  $\langle\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}B,A\rangle_{1/2}=\langle B,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A\rangle_{1/2}$  for all  $A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$ .
Thus,  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is the adjoint of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with respect to the  $\sigma$ -KMS inner product, and  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is a completely positive operator on  $\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})$  such that  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}({{\bf 1}})={{\bf 1}}$  and  $(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma$ .
Define a quantum Markov semigroup  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  by
${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\frac{t^{n}}{n!}(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})^{n}=e^{t(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}-I)}\ .$
Evidently  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  is KMS-symmetric for each  $t>0$  since  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is KMS-symmetric. Furthermore,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  commutes with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  for each  $t>0$  if and only if  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  commutes with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
We will show that the latter is not generally the case.
To construct counterexamples, consider  $n=2$ ; the construction that follows is
readily generalized. Let  $\{u_{1},u_{2}\}$  be an orthonormal basis in  ${\mathbb{C}}^{2}$  and let  $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$  be a set of two linearly independent unit vectors in  ${\mathbb{C}}^{2}$  that are not orthogonal.
Define the rank-one operators
$K_{1}$  and  $K_{2}$  by  $K_{j}=|v_{j}\rangle\langle u_{j}|$ ,  $j=1,2$ .
Evidently,  $K_{1}^{*}K_{1}+K_{2}^{*}K_{2}={{\bf 1}}$ ,
and we define  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A=K_{1}^{*}AK_{1}+K_{2}^{*}AK_{2}$  so that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}$ .
Then the range of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}$  is spanned by
$\big\{|v_{1}\rangle\langle v_{1}|\ ,\,|v_{2}\rangle\langle v_{2}|\big\}$ .
A simple computation yields
${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\big(\alpha_{1}|v_{1}\rangle\langle v_{1}|+\alpha_{2}|v_{2}\rangle\langle v_{2}|\big)=\beta_{1}|v_{1}\rangle\langle v_{1}|+\beta_{2}|v_{2}\rangle\langle v_{2}|\ ,$
where
(B.1)
$\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\beta_{1}\\
\beta_{2}\end{array}\right)=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}1-a&b\\
a&1-b\end{array}\right]\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\alpha_{1}\\
\alpha_{2}\end{array}\right)\ ,$
with  $a=|\langle v_{1},u_{2}\rangle|^{2}$  and  $b=|\langle v_{2},u_{1}\rangle|^{2}$ ,
and since  $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$  is not orthogonal,  $a+b>0$ .
The vector  $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}b\\
a\end{array}\right)$  is an eigenvector
with eigenvalue  $1$ , and hence
(B.2)
$\sigma=\frac{b}{a+b}|v_{1}\rangle\langle v_{1}|+\frac{a}{a+b}|v_{2}\rangle\langle v_{2}|$
satisfies  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma$ , and hence, as we just noted,  $(\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma$ .
The other eigenvalue of the matrix in (B.1) is  $1-a-b<1$ , so that (B.2) gives the unique invariant state.
It follows that the eigenvalues of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}$  are  $1$ ,  $1-a-b$
and  $0$ , with
${\rm Null}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger})={\rm Span}\big\{|u_{1}\rangle\langle u_{2}|\ ,\ |u_{2}\rangle\langle u_{1}|\big\}\ .$
Consequently, the null space of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is  $2$ -dimensional as well, and same holds for the null space of  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$ , since  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  is the  $\sigma$ -KMS dual of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$ .
By ergodicity, it is the only eigenspace of  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with this property.
Generically,  $\sigma$  will have two distinct eigenvalues. (For example, take  $\{u_{1},u_{2}\}$  to be the standard basis of  ${\mathbb{C}}^{2}$ , and take  $v_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\
1\end{array}\right)$  and
$v_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\
2\end{array}\right)$ , so that
$\sigma=\frac{1}{7}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2&3\\
3&5\end{array}\right]$ .)
Let  $\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$  be an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of  $\sigma$ .
If  ${\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}$  and  $\Delta_{\sigma}$  were to commute, then Remark 2.7 would imply that  $|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|$  and  $|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|$  are linearly independent eigenvectors of  $\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$  with the same eigenvalue.
This eigenvalue can only be zero by the above. But then  $0={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|)={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|)$ .
Hence we would have
$0={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|)=\langle v_{1},\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1},v_{1}\rangle|u_{1}\rangle\langle u_{1}|+\langle v_{2},\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1},v_{2}\rangle|u_{2}\rangle\langle u_{2}|\ ,$
which would mean that
(B.3)
$\langle v_{1},\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1},v_{1}\rangle=0\quad{\rm and}\quad\langle v_{2},\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1},v_{2}\rangle=0\ .$
Suppose  $\langle v_{1},\eta_{2}\rangle=0$ .
Then since  $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$  is not orthogonal, and  $\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$  is,  $\langle v_{2},\eta_{1}\rangle\neq 0$ .
The second equality in (B.3) then yields  $\langle v_{2},\eta_{2}\rangle$ , but we cannot have both  $\langle v_{1},\eta_{2}\rangle=0$  and  $\langle v_{2},\eta_{2}\rangle=0$  since this would imply that  $\eta_{2}=0$ .
Under this condition, the first equality in (B.3) would yield  $\langle\eta_{1},v_{1}\rangle=0$ . As above, this would imply
$\langle\eta_{2},v_{2}\rangle\neq 0$ , and hence  $\langle\eta_{1},v_{2}\rangle=0$ . We cannot have both
$\langle v_{1},\eta_{1}\rangle=0$  and  $\langle v_{2},\eta_{1}\rangle=0$  since this would imply that  $\eta_{1}=0$ .
Hence  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|)=0$  is impossible.
Thus, with this choice of  ${\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}$ ,  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}:=\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}-I$  is the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup with invariant state  $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}$  such that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is self-adjoint with respect to the  $\sigma$ -KMS inner product
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}$ , but such that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  does not commute with  $\Delta_{\sigma}$ .
It follows that  ${\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}$  is not self-adjoint with respect to the GNS inner product.
